items.descriptionOriginal: A former Los Angeles gang member, a former skinhead and a former radical Islamist walk into a youth center. What sounds like the setup for an uneasy joke is at the core of Farah Pandith’s work: Put people who might otherwise never share a room in front of young people; let them explain what drew them into extremism and how they found their way out. “They’re the most authentic and credible voices there are,” Pandith says. More than once she has observed that their stories reach an audience that official warnings cannot. For decades, including while working for the U.S. government under the Obama, George W. Bush and George H.W. Bush administrations, Pandith researched why people embrace ideologies that divide the world into “us versus them.” Before people can be persuaded away from hatred, she argues, one has to understand what they are looking for: recognition, certainty or a place in the world. “You don’t suddenly explode and become an extremist overnight. You’re having some self-doubt, you’re asking questions about who you are,” she says from her light-filled living room in Arlington, Virginia. Preventing someone from becoming an extremist has been her lifelong goal, because it’s “infinitely easier than dealing with the fallout.” Farah Pandith visits the Indonesian city of Bekasi during her time as the U.S. special representative to Muslim communities. Credit: U.S. Embassy, Jakarta / Wikimedia Commons While working for the government, she traveled to nearly 100 countries, from Belgium to Bangladesh, to understand how extremists’ descent into violence can be interrupted. Today she applies what she learned to a broader problem: how to make compassion more than an admirable sentiment and help communities put it into practice. Last year Pandith received the ADL Daniel Pearl Award , which is given annually to a person who has had a positive impact on understanding between Jews and the Muslim world, and is sponsored by the parents of the journalist who was kidnapped and killed in Pakistan in 2002. “It is hard to think of anyone more knowledgeable than Farah Pandith when it comes to countering violent extremism,” Joseph Nye, the late chair of the National Intelligence Council, said about her. On September 11, 2001, Pandith watched on television like millions of others as two planes struck the World Trade Center. “It felt very heavy,” she recalls, putting a hand to her heart. “The world kind of went still for a moment, like, ‘What do we do about this?’” She felt compelled to act, to help prevent such violence from happening again. She especially rejected the way extremists attempted to define her religion on the airwaves. “Who are they to dictate what Islam is?” she remembers thinking. “For me, Islam means humility, compassion, to treat others with respect.” Initially, when she worked for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), cooperating with local organizations showed her that effective policy depends on understanding the people on the ground. “You have to listen really well to find a solution that matches with the local community,” she says. “That’s tricky and complex. Trust has to be built first.” The same principle, she realized, applied to preventing violent extremism. Government officials could not design effective strategies from Washington alone. They needed to hear from the people they hoped to reach, including those whose voices had been overlooked. After joining the National Security Council in 2004, Pandith helped develop the “soft power” side of the Global War on Terror through a new approach called Countering Violent Extremism. Military action might disrupt extremist organizations, but it could not prevent them from recruiting new members. Nor were public relations campaigns successful in overcoming the distrust of Muslims worldwide. Even in her own government, distrust was impossible to ignore. One congressman called the White House to complain a “jihadist” was sitting in the Council. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Pandith was briefly living in Afghanistan’s capital, Kabul, in 2004 when photographs of abuse at Abu Ghraib surfaced showing American soldiers humiliating Muslim prisoners. “In an instant, all our efforts on the ground were harmed irreparably,” she says. Locals asked how she could represent a government that treated Muslim prisoners that way. The experience reinforced a lesson: Building trust also meant receiving criticism, sitting through uncomfortable conversations. Pandith carried that approach into her work at the State Department, where Hillary Clinton appointed her the first U.S. special representative to Muslim communities in 2009. Instead of treating Muslim populations as a single audience for American messages, she traveled widely, meeting people in homes, mosques and community settings to learn what mattered to them. “You have to go to the rural areas,” she says, aiming to support credible local voices that could offer alternatives to extremist narratives. Pandith herself has been shaped by a background that made her an ideal diplomat. She came to the U.S. from Kashmir as a baby with her mother, a pulmonologist and the medical director of a hospital. Pandith describes growing up in a highly educated Muslim family without experiencing discrimination. She remembers an America in which people of different faiths could live alongside one another, “with a synagogue, a church, a mosque and a temple in the same part of town.” Today, she admits, that harmonious coexistence feels nearly impossible. Her parents separated when she was 10, and her mother raised Pandith and her brother on her own. One of her greatest influences was her uncle, a heart surgeon. “I’ve held the hearts of different people in my hands,” he would tell her. “Always remember: There is no difference between the heart of a Muslim, a Jew, a Hindu or a Christian.” Pandith feels she carries “many identities” — an American, a woman, a Muslim and a foreign policy professional, among others. “I have a face that people can’t quite know where I’m from,” she explains. “Sometimes people think I’m Italian.” She also relies on what she calls her “superpower” when speaking with Muslims. When she tells them she was born in Kashmir, the atmosphere often changes. “Suddenly I’m like a sister to them.” Farah Pandith on a panel at the Milken Institute Asia Summit. Courtesy of Farah Pandith Her ability to forge connections would become one of her greatest professional assets. By chance, Barbara Bush, the wife of President George H.W. Bush, visited Smith College during Farah’s senior year. She was so impressed by a speech Pandith gave as student body president that she helped her secure her job at USAID after graduation. That was how the young woman began traveling around the world. Pandith’s work challenged conventional explanations of radicalization. Poverty and lack of education, she argued, could not explain why people embraced violent ideologies. Some of the 9/11 terrorists were well educated. Pandith pointed to a different cause she observed in Muslim communities: deep identity crises among young people who struggled to find their place in a rapidly changing world. She thinks of a young woman in Denmark whose Imam told her she wasn’t a Muslim if she didn’t cover her head. Or Mubin Shaikh in Canada, who went to Pakistan and Syria as a 19-year-old to fight alongside the jihadists and who now teaches security politics at the University of Ottawa. Pandith has seen firsthand that dialogue can change minds. ““It’s less interesting for the media than an extremist’s video, but the conversations we had affected people.” Her initiatives have sought to make dialogue a shared responsibility. Against Violent Extremism became the world’s first and only network of former extremists, launched by the U.S. Department of State, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and Google. The “Hours Against Hate” campaign encouraged teenagers to spend an hour doing something for someone different from themselves. Millions participated. Sisters Against Violent Extremism connected mothers concerned about their children’s vulnerability to extremist recruitment. In a citizen-dialogue program, Pandith traveled through Europe with other Muslim Americans to share experiences and listen to local concerns. People had the chance to meet someone they might otherwise see only through stereotypes and to develop a relationship that complicated those assumptions. In her book How We Win , recently reissued, Pandith remains stubbornly optimistic: The fight against extremism can be won. Preventing people from being drawn into extremist movements requires intervening early and bringing together the people who can reach them — not just government officials, but business leaders, teachers, local communities and influencers whose networks, knowledge and credibility government agencies lack. “The fight against violent extremism is not going to be won solely by the efforts of government,” she argues. “We need businesses to step up as never before, for the public interest as well as their own.” She insists that this work cannot be dismissed as idealism or do-goodery but is “a matter of national security” — as important as the hard power of military force. Pandith emphasizes that the underlying lessons extend beyond Islamist extremism. The same dynamics of exclusion and dehumanization can fuel hostility toward religious minorities, LGBTQ+ people and Asian communities, among others. Still, she admits that the strategies for countering violent extremism never fully came to fruition, often mired in bureaucracy. “Congress provided just 0.0138 percent of funding compared to the funding for the military,” she calculates. “We know what we need to do. We spent 25 years researching and exchanging strategies. But we left the field to the extremists.” Pandith sees the reality as a call to action: “We cannot just wring our hands and keep saying things are bad and things are difficult and somebody else’s problem. We need everybody.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime She now works outside government to advance another part of this agenda, as senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations , teaching countering violent extremism at Georgetown University, and as a Global Peace Laureate for the Muhammad Ali Center. She has been developing the Muhammad Ali Index on compassion . For Pandith, compassion is the capacity to recognize another person’s humanity even amid disagreement, and to resist the impulse to turn differences into a reason for contempt. “There isn’t a faith on planet Earth that doesn’t have compassion in it. And even if you are not religious you understand what it means, right?” As part of the Muhammed Ali Index, more than 5,400 people in 12 American cities responded to the 2025 State of Compassion survey . Sixty-one percent said they felt compassion has declined in the last four years, but 43 percent were optimistic about the future of compassion in America. A second index, planned for 2027, will cover 20 U.S. cities and 12 cities around the world. The ambition is practical. Pandith hopes the data will help mayors, school leaders, faith groups and local organizations identify opportunities to build stronger connections and design efforts suited to their own communities. The point is not to prescribe a universal program, but to create a framework that can be adapted. “We want to see people taking inspiration from the data to actually do something over time so we can measure and see what takes place,” she says passionately, insisting that compassion can be trained: “Compassion is a muscle that can be exercised.” Yet the starting point is personal: “Self-compassion is essential.” Building the capacity for compassion, Pandith argues, begins with recognizing what is happening inside oneself. She is particularly interested in reaching young people early. “The world that they are growing up in is so polarized and so difficult and so different from the one that we have grown up in,” she says, “that they don’t have a memory of people who are different from them speaking to each other with dignity regularly.” As Pandith sees it, waiting for polarization to disappear on its own is not a strategy. The task is to build relationships and connections that open up hearts and minds — and to keep investing in them long enough to learn what works. She repeats her favorite sentence: “Solutions are available and affordable.” UPDATE — November 3, 2026: This story has been updated to clarify facts about Pandith’s work and background. items.descriptionOriginal: When Suhani Gupta and her sister spot more than seven stars from their balcony in Gurugram, they have a reason to celebrate. They step outside, open Stellarium, an astronomy app, and try to identify the constellations above them. In a city where the night sky rarely offers a clear view of the stars, even a handful can turn an ordinary evening into an occasion. "My sister and I get excited when we see more than seven stars in the sky," Suhani tells The Better India. The sisters initially assumed that air pollution was responsible for the limited visibility. After all, Gurugram frequently experiences haze. But visits to her grandparents in Udhampur, Jammu and Kashmir , offered Suhani a different perspective. The sky there appeared far more generous with stars. The stars had not suddenly multiplied in the mountains. Something about the surroundings had changed. That difference led Suhani to investigate light pollution — the excessive or poorly directed use of artificial light that brightens the night sky and makes celestial objects harder to see. Buildings, roads, commercial establishments and other sources of outdoor lighting can contribute to this glow. The consequences extend beyond astronomy, affecting nocturnal wildlife, ecosystems and human exposure to darkness. Unlike a polluted river or a visible plume of smoke, an increasingly bright night sky can be difficult to recognise as an environmental change. Photograph: (Alexey Elfimov) But how could a school student measure a problem that even many adults rarely recognise? In May 2025, Suhani, now a Class 12 student, began teaching herself image processing and developing SkyQi, a free online platform that estimates night-sky quality using photographs taken on smartphones . The project has since grown into a citizen-science initiative, attracting observations from users across dozens of countries. In 2026, she took the investigation further. Using NASA satellite data, she examined changes in night-time radiance across 50 Indian cities between 2015 and 2025. Her analysis found that the median city's measured night-time radiance was 70% higher in 2025 than in 2015, while 47 of the 50 cities recorded an increase. Leh, known for its dark skies and astronomy tourism, showed the steepest rise in her dataset, at 546%. The findings do not directly measure how bright the sky appears to someone standing on the ground. They do, however, raise questions about how urban growth, tourism and outdoor lighting are changing India's nights. For Suhani, the aim is to make those changes easier to observe, understand and eventually address. From a school astronomy club to a pollution problem Suhani's interest in light pollution began in 2024, when she was part of her school's space society. During meteor showers and other astronomical events, members would gather on voice chat at around 3 am to watch the sky. Observing the stars required patience. Participants would spend about 30 minutes outside, allowing their eyes to adjust to the darkness before attempting to identify celestial objects. "While we generally do that to adjust to the moon's brightness, the haze in our sky was much more, and that is kind of how I got into light pollution," she explains. She began watching YouTube videos and reading research on the effects of artificial light on human health, wildlife, ecosystems and astronomy. Suhani had previously worked with Arduinos and Raspberry Pi and built a visual aid for people who are blind using vision-language models and computer vision. Photograph: (Suhani Gupta; Getty Images) "Unlike other forms of pollution, air, water, or even noise, light pollution came on gradually, so we never even knew it was taking over our skies," she says. Unlike a polluted river or a visible plume of smoke, an increasingly bright night sky can be difficult to recognise as an environmental change. New buildings, illuminated advertisements, streetlights and commercial spaces may appear to make a city safer or more developed. Yet the cumulative effect of unnecessary or poorly directed lighting can reduce the darkness that once allowed people to see the stars. Suhani wanted to understand how this gradual change could be measured. She also wanted to find a method that did not require expensive equipment or specialised astronomical knowledge. Can a smartphone measure the night sky? Professional astronomers use instruments called Sky Quality Meters to measure the brightness of the night sky. These devices provide numerical readings that help observers assess how dark a location is. However, their cost can put them beyond the reach of students, amateur astronomers and community groups. Suhani began exploring whether an ordinary smartphone camera could offer an alternative. She was not entirely new to technology. She had previously worked with Arduinos and Raspberry Pi and built a visual aid for people who are blind using vision-language models and computer vision. Her parents helped her develop the skills required for the project. Both are software engineers from BITS Pilani, and her mother had worked on image processing for Nokia phones. "My mom taught me the concepts, and a lot more Python along the way," Suhani says. She reworked the platform to assess three indicators: the number of visible stars, the difference in brightness between the horizon and the sky directly overhead, and the calculated brightness of the sky. She supplemented these lessons with research papers, programming libraries and help from her father. She also used AI as a learning aid while trying to understand the techniques astronomers use to assess the night sky, including the Bortle scale. The Bortle scale classifies night skies according to their darkness and the visibility of stars and other celestial objects. At one end are heavily light-polluted urban skies; at the other are exceptionally dark skies where the Milky Way and faint celestial objects are visible. Suhani began developing SkyQi in May 2025. The first version assessed a photograph's overall brightness and converted it into a score. But the results were unreliable. A cloudy sky could be mistaken for a light-polluted one. A camera sensor could count bright pixels as stars, while overexposed photographs could distort the readings. "I realised that one measurement wasn't enough," she says. She reworked the platform to assess three indicators: the number of visible stars, the difference in brightness between the horizon and the sky directly overhead, and the calculated brightness of the sky. The platform compares these measurements to determine whether they broadly agree. If they do, it assigns a confidence level to the reading. If they do not, the result can be flagged as less reliable. SkyQi went live in September 2025. However, making the platform available was only the beginning. Suhani soon found that its formula classified too many photographs, including some taken in towns, as almost perfectly dark because the calculation had reached its measurement ceiling. She revised the method to account for information recorded by smartphone cameras, particularly shutter speed and ISO settings. "Two phones can photograph the same sky and produce very different-looking pictures, and a longer exposure makes the sky look brighter, so knowing the settings lets me correct for that," she explains. When these details are missing, as can happen when photographs are forwarded through WhatsApp or edited, SkyQi uses a published world atlas of light pollution as a starting point and adjusts the estimate using information from the photograph. It labels such results as 'Estimated'. The platform also checks cloud forecasts for the location and flags observations that may have been affected by clouds. The system is still evolving. SkyQi currently uses a shared calibration across phone models, while model-specific calibration remains part of Suhani's plans. What makes a reading reliable? Clouds can obscure stars while reflecting artificial light towards the ground. Moonlight can brighten the sky, while camera movement can blur stars or make them difficult to identify. Smartphone image processing can further alter the apparent brightness of a photograph. So SkyQi does not rely on a single indicator. It compares the three measurements and assigns high, medium or low confidence according to how consistently they point towards the same conclusion. A high-confidence reading does not guarantee that the result is correct. It means that the available indicators agree with one another. Suhani has tested an earlier version of the platform against 104 reference night-sky images with known Bortle classifications. According to her, SkyQi's result was within one Bortle class of the reference approximately 65% of the time. However, the tool has not yet been validated against a professional Sky Quality Meter. "I do not possess a professional sky quality meter but one that I made by myself using an Arduino. Thus, I haven't compared it yet with a professional Sky Quality Meter," she tells The Better India. A few hundred photographs containing complete camera settings have been submitted since September, and Suhani hopes to use these observations to improve the platform's calibration. For now, she describes SkyQi as a citizen-science tool rather than a substitute for professional instruments. Its value lies partly in helping people collect observations from different locations and, ideally, repeat them over time. She recommends photographing the sky on clear nights, preferably when the Moon is not visible and at least an hour and a half after sunset. Users should move away from direct light sources, keep their phones steady, point towards an open sky and upload original, unedited photographs. What did 50 Indian cities reveal? Once SkyQi was underway, Suhani turned to a larger question: had India's night skies become brighter over the previous decade? In 2026, she analysed NASA satellite data covering 50 Indian cities in 2015, 2020 and 2025. Her report found that the median city's measured night-time radiance was 70% higher in 2025 than in 2015. Forty-seven cities recorded an increase over the period. Leh stood out, with satellite-observed night-time radiance rising by 546%, according to her analysis. "Leh is one of the only dark sky places left in our country, and despite it being such a remote high-altitude place, we observe light pollution levels increasing," she says. The finding raises particular concerns because Leh and the wider Ladakh region are associated with high-altitude landscapes, astronomy and relatively dark skies. Suhani points to urbanisation and the growth of tourism infrastructure as possible contributors to increasing artificial light. Hotels, homestays, restaurants and other facilities have expanded in places that were previously less developed. A few hundred photographs containing complete camera settings have been submitted since September, and Suhani hopes to use these observations to improve the platform's calibration. This creates a paradox. Visitors travel to Ladakh to experience its night sky, but the infrastructure built to accommodate them can introduce additional artificial light. Communities around Hanle, for instance, have developed homestays and astronomy-related tourism, with residents training to welcome visitors as astronomy guides, sometimes known as Astro Ambassadors. Protecting dark skies could therefore be important not only for astronomical research but also for a tourism economy that depends on them. However, the figures require careful interpretation. "The analysis that suggested a 546% increase was in satellite-observed nighttime radiance from 2015 to now, and while satellite radiance is not a direct measure of ground-level sky brightness, the stark increase suggests a drastic increase even in ground-level sky brightness," Suhani says. What's next for Suhani? Suhani has made her report and the underlying city-level dataset publicly available, allowing other researchers and interested readers to examine the figures. According to the latest figures she shared with The Better India, the platform has received 1,198 photographs from more than 490 contributors across 63 countries. "I was initially skeptical of the reach SkyQi would attain and continue to remain amazed at how many people have tried the tool out," she says. India is currently the third-largest source of readings on the platform, after the United States and China. "The ultimate aim of SkyQi has always been to find or build a community of people passionate about light pollution advocacy and spread awareness about it, and it has achieved exactly that," she says. She hopes schools and astronomy clubs will organise night-sky surveys in which students photograph the sky from the same locations month after month. Repeated observations could help participants identify patterns and locations that need more detailed investigation. For now, the project asks people to do something simple: look up, take a photograph and pay attention to what the sky reveals. "Light pollution isn't something we just have to live with," she says. The question that began on a Gurugram balcony has now expanded to 50 Indian cities and a growing international community of observers . What started as an attempt to understand why the stars looked different in Udhampur has become an effort to measure how artificial light is changing the night.

items.descriptionOriginal: Some bees line their nests with soft petals. Some line them with hardened tree sap. Some line them with a thin, flexible film composed of silk and polyester. And this latter group—known as cellophane bees—may hold the key to sustainable, biodegradable plastic, according to a new study. “Nature has already solved a problem that polymer scientists are still working on: a bioplastic that is chemically and physically similar to conventional plastics but doesn’t persist in the environment,” says study team member Jonathan Coote , assistant professor in the Department of Sustainable Biomaterials at Virginia Tech University. Unlike more familiar hive-dwelling honeybees, cellophane bees nest in the soil. Females lay eggs in individual chambers that they line with secretions from a gland on their abdomen. Scientists have known for almost half a century that this lining is composed of silk fibers and a polyester similar to polyethylene—a material that makes up about one-third of human-produced plastics and is the most commonly used plastic for packaging. “Polyethylene-like polyesters made in the lab generally don’t break down well in the environment,” says Coote. “The bees’ material, however, breaks down rapidly in soil.” Although the bees nest in aggregations of 10,000 or more individual nests and often use the same nest sites for decades, their habitat never becomes choked with plastic—in contrast to large aggregations of modern humans. To find out more about how the bees do it, Coote and his collaborators gathered nest linings from two Tennessee nest sites of a species of cellophane bee known as Colletes inaequalis . They put the material through a battery of tests to characterize its structure and chemical makeup. They also collected nest linings that had been in the ground for four, seven, and 11 months to track how the material degrades over time. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby The tradeoff at the heart of bioplastics. A fresh nest cell lining is about 73% polyester and 27% silk by weight, the researchers report. The polyester is semicrystalline, likely has cross-linked polymer chains, and has a crystal structure and degradation temperature similar to that of polyethylene. “The biggest surprise was that the material is most likely cross-linked, meaning its polymer chains are chemically tied together into a network,” says Coote. “Cross-linked plastics, called thermosets, are typically very durable, and designing thermosets that break down at the end of their life is a major challenge in polymer science. So finding a thermoset that breaks down rapidly in soil was very counterintuitive, and it’s exciting to have a natural example to learn from.” By four months, the nest linings are just 40% polyester, meaning that the polyester degrades even more rapidly than famously biodegradable silk in the first months (after that, the composition changes much more slowly). Four-month-old nest linings remain flexible and intact, protecting the nest cell from moisture and microbes like a shrink-wrapped bell pepper at the grocery store. By seven months, about the time the larva has developed into an adult bee, the lining easily cracks easily; by 11 months, it crumbles in the hand. In other words, unlike that bell pepper’s shrink wrap, the nest lining lasts just as long as is needed to protect the developing bee, and no longer. The researchers next aim to investigate how the material breaks down so quickly. They hypothesize that the particularities of polyester’s crystal structure may leave the bonds that connect the material’s subunits exposed to a greater degree than in other polyesters. There’s also evidence of an enzyme that breaks these bonds present in the nest lining, perhaps from the mother bee’s saliva. “The goal is to reverse engineer what the bees are doing so that we can design similar materials in the lab and eventually produce them at practical scale,” Coote says. items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can't always answer. As the evening sky turns dark, little diyas begin to flicker along balconies and windowsills. Inside one Faridabad home, the preparations for Diwali are a little different. Three-year-old Rishaan Garg Batra is getting ready to celebrate with his parents, Neha Garg and Siddhant Batra, and his four furry siblings, the family's dogs. There are diyas to light, a family photograph to take, friends and relatives to meet, games to play and , of course, plenty of good food to look forward to. There is one thing missing from the celebrations, though: firecrackers. There is also no last-minute rush to buy new clothes or festive decorations. Growing up with four furry siblings, three-year-old Rishaan is learning why firecrackers can frighten animals and harm the environment. For Neha, a podcaster, writer and brand strategist, and Siddhant, an IT and sports entrepreneur, Diwali has always been about the simple joys of being together. The couple has never been particularly drawn to loud celebrations or the idea of buying something new for every occasion. Over the years, they have built their own little traditions around the festival of lights, and now they are bringing up Rishaan with the same understanding. For Rishaan, this is what Diwali looks like: a few lights, familiar faces, meals shared with loved ones and memories made together. 2 childhood experiences that changed how they celebrate Diwali Neha and Siddhant had each grown uncomfortable with firecrackers long before becoming parents, though for different reasons. Siddhant's turning point came when his sister spoke to him about child labour associated with the manufacture of firecrackers. The two siblings decided to stop bursting them around Grades 5 or 6. Eventually, the rest of the family also adopted a low-noise Diwali. Neha, on the other hand, grew up in a large joint family where firecrackers were an important part of the festivities. Every year, a huge stock would be purchased and divided among the different family units, with each child receiving their share. But she was never particularly fond of them. "I just didn't like the loudness and the cloud of smoke that is left behind after we burst them," she recalls. Something else stayed with her, too. Her mother suffered from severe allergies because of the smoke. While the rest of the family went upstairs to burst crackers, her mother would often remain in the kitchen, coughing and struggling with the fumes. From reusing festive outfits to skipping unnecessary shopping, Neha and Siddhant are teaching their son that celebrations need not come with new purchases. "Seeing her, I would feel really triggered, and I would always wonder, why are we doing this if this is making her so uncomfortable?" says Neha. Instead of joining the others, she would stay back with her mother and help prepare the elaborate Diwali meal. As they grew older, both began to understand the wider consequences of the practice, from air and noise pollution to the distress it causes animals. Being dog lovers, the latter was particularly difficult for them to overlook. When they eventually came together as a couple, not bursting firecrackers was simply something they agreed on. '90% of our kid's wardrobe is preloved pieces' Another thing that Neha and Siddhant have never associated with festivals is shopping. Despite growing up in very different family settings, both had similar ideas about buying new clothes for special occasions. For Neha, weddings were when new clothes were usually purchased. With several weddings taking place in her extended family, there were always outfits that could be reused for festivals. Siddhant, too, never really understood the idea that every festival had to come with a new wardrobe. In fact, he would find it difficult to relate to school essays that described buying new clothes as an essential part of festive celebrations. Today, the couple follows the same approach at home. "We wear clothes we already own, restyle outfits and avoid shopping simply because a festival is around the corner," says Neha. Lighting diyas together is one of the family's favourite Diwali traditions, bringing everyone together for a moment of prayer. Instead, if they choose to spend on something, it is usually food or an experience they can enjoy with family and friends. "Food is a big, big part of how we celebrate and how we see celebrations and how we see togetherness. And if at all our money goes in anything material, it goes on food," Neha says. The same thinking extends to Rishaan's wardrobe. Since he was born, the couple has consciously encouraged friends and family to give him preloved clothes instead of buying new ones. Today, nearly 90 per cent of his wardrobe consists of preloved pieces, including everyday outfits, party wear and traditional clothes such as kurtas . For Neha and Siddhant, this is not something they practise only during Diwali. It is a lifestyle choice they want their son to grow up considering perfectly normal . Growing up with four furry siblings At home, some of Rishaan's earliest lessons about being mindful come through his relationship with the family's four dogs. The little one knows that firecrackers can frighten his furry siblings and that the smoke and noise affect animals around them. He has also begun understanding why his parents choose not to burst crackers. Siddhant says Rishaan sometimes takes it upon himself to explain this to others. "If he sees people burning crackers, he goes up to them and says that, you know, this is a bad thing. You should not do it; it causes pollution." Food, family games and visits to friends and relatives make up the celebrations in the Garg Batra household, without the noise of firecrackers. The couple makes it a point to explain the reasoning behind their choices rather than simply asking Rishaan to follow certain rules. They talk to him about what happens when people burst firecrackers, why buying things unnecessarily adds to waste, and what they are choosing when they decide to celebrate differently. For them, he must understand the thought behind these decisions. "Kids are not dumb people. They are very intelligent. They understand if you explain to them logically why you're doing what you're doing," Neha says. A family photograph that includes everyone While Neha and Siddhant prefer simple Diwali celebrations, one family tradition has grown more meaningful as their family has grown. One of their favourite rituals is an annual family photograph. It includes the couple, Rishaan, their four dogs and photographs of the three dogs who have passed away. The tradition began quite spontaneously when it was just Neha, Siddhant and their first two dogs, Koch and Maya. As their family grew, so did the photograph. When one of their dogs passed away, they decided to include his picture in the frame. The tradition has continued ever since. The family's annual Diwali photograph includes Neha, Siddhant, Rishaan and their four dogs, along with pictures of the three pets they have lost. Today, the photograph is a way of bringing the entire family together, including the furry members who are no longer around. Another ritual they have created is lighting diyas together. On Diwali evening, the family gathers around the lights, takes turns praying and then prays together. "We just pray to the light because it is a festival of light. So on that evening, we light diyas and we pray as a family and we pray as individuals to whatever force there might be," Neha shares. The rest of the day is spent visiting friends and relatives, eating good food and playing games such as Tambola, cards and Dumb Charades. There is no elaborate checklist to get through or pressure to make the day look a certain way. Just time spent with people they love. The little traditions they want their son to carry forward Neha says that becoming parents has made Diwali more meaningful for them. Earlier, the couple was happy keeping the festival simple. Now, they want to create memories and traditions that Rishaan can look forward to every year. Living in Faridabad, they are also aware of the pollution that surrounds the festive season. The family hopes to eventually spend Diwali somewhere less polluted and noisy, away from the city's festivities, although they have not managed to put that plan into action yet. When asked what she hopes Rishaan remembers about Diwali when he grows up, Neha doesn't talk about the things they chose to leave out. Instead, she hopes he remembers the happiness, the food, the games, the family photographs and the time spent with friends and loved ones. By explaining the reasons behind their choices, Neha and Siddhant hope Rishaan grows up making mindful decisions of his own. And for parents who might want to make their celebrations more mindful but worry that their children will miss out, she has a thought drawn from her own experience. "Children miss out on only what they know. If they know your way, they will not miss out on any other way." For Neha and Siddhant, the hope is that Rishaan grows up understanding the reasons behind their choices and finding happiness in the traditions they share. For this family, Diwali is about lighting a few diyas , gathering everyone for that much-loved photograph and making sure there is always room at the table for one more. items.title: Οι επιστήμονες ανακαλύπτουν μια εκπληκτική ένδειξη για την προέλευση του αυτισμού που κρύβεται στον πλακούντα

items.description: Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν μια απροσδόκητη σχέση μεταξύ της φλεγμονής κατά τη διάρκεια της εγκυμοσύνης, της βλάβης του πλακούντα και των χαρακτηριστικών που μοιάζουν με αυτισμό σε αρσενικά ποντίκια, ενώ τα θηλυκά φαινόταν φυσικά προστατευμένα. Η ανακάλυψη θα μπορούσε να εξηγήσει γιατί ο αυτισμός διαγιγνώσκεται πιο συχνά στα αγόρια και να αποκαλύψει νέες ευκαιρίες για έγκαιρη παρέμβαση.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between inflammation during pregnancy, placental damage, and autism-like traits in male mice, while females appeared naturally protected. The discovery could help explain why autism is diagnosed more frequently in boys and reveal new opportunities for early intervention.

items.titleOriginal: Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day
items.description: Η κατανάλωση ενός αβοκάντο και ενός φλιτζάνι μάνγκο κάθε μέρα μπορεί να προσφέρει εκπληκτικά οφέλη για την υγεία της καρδιάς, σύμφωνα με μια νέα μελέτη στην οποία συμμετείχαν ενήλικες με προδιαβήτη. Μετά από μόλις οκτώ εβδομάδες, οι συμμετέχοντες παρουσίασαν σημαντικές βελτιώσεις στη λειτουργία των αιμοφόρων αγγείων και στη διαστολική αρτηριακή πίεση, ιδιαίτερα στους άνδρες. Αυτά τα οφέλη προέκυψαν χωρίς βάρος g…
items.descriptionOriginal: Eating an avocado and a cup of mango every day may provide surprising benefits for heart health, according to a new study involving adults with prediabetes. After just eight weeks, participants experienced significant improvements in blood vessel function and diastolic blood pressure, particularly among men. These benefits occurred without weight gain or changes in calorie intake, suggesting that the nutrient-rich combination could support cardiovascular health through a simple dietary adjustment.

items.title: Οι επιστήμονες εντοπίζουν δύο παραγνωρισμένες δεξιότητες που προβλέπουν επιτυχία στην ανάγνωση
items.titleOriginal: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
items.description: Μια τεράστια νέα μελέτη αποκαλύπτει ότι η νοημοσύνη παίζει έναν εκπληκτικά περιορισμένο ρόλο στην επιτυχία των παιδιών στην ανάγνωση, ενώ η οπτική επεξεργασία δεν έδειξε καμία ουσιαστική σχέση. Αντίθετα, οι ισχυρότεροι προγνωστικοί παράγοντες είναι η αναγνώριση ήχου, το λεξιλόγιο και η γνώση του υποβάθρου, προσφέροντας νέες ενδείξεις σχετικά με το πώς να βοηθήσετε τους αναγνώστες που αγωνίζονται.
items.descriptionOriginal: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

items.descriptionOriginal: *Γράφει η personal trainer, κυρία Σοφία Περδίκη Η φυσική άσκηση βρίσκεται σε μια περίοδο μετάβασης. Η τεχνητή νοημοσύνη (AI) αλλάζει τον τρόπο με τον οποίο σχεδιάζονται τα προγράμματα, παρακολουθείται η απόδοση και η εξέλιξη, αξιολογούνται τα δεδομένα και καθοδηγούνται οι ασκούμενοι. Το κρίσιμο ερώτημα, όμως, δεν είναι αν το AI μπορεί να δημιουργήσει ένα πρόγραμμα γυμναστικής. Είναι αν μπορεί να προσφέρει την ποιότητα καθοδήγησης που απαιτεί το ανθρώπινο σώμα και αν η τεχνολογία βελτιώνει πραγματικά την άσκηση ή απλώς την κάνει πιο εύκολα προσβάσιμη. Η γυμναστική γίνεται πιο εξατομικευμένη και μετρήσιμη Η αλλαγή δεν είναι θεωρητική. Στην ετήσια έρευνα του American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) για τις τάσεις του 2025 , η φορετή τεχνολογία κατέλαβε την πρώτη θέση, οι εφαρμογές άσκησης τη δεύτερη και η τεχνολογία προπόνησης βάσει δεδομένων την έβδομη. Η έρευνα βασίστηκε σε περίπου 2.000 επαγγελματίες και ερευνητές του χώρου. Αυτό δείχνει ότι η τεχνολογία δεν αποτελεί πλέον περιφερειακό εργαλείο της γυμναστικής . Ενσωματώνεται στον τρόπο με τον οποίο σχεδιάζονται και αξιολογούνται οι προπονήσεις. Οι σημαντικότερες αλλαγές είναι οι εξής: Εξατομίκευση Τα εργαλεία AI μπορούν να προτείνουν κάποιο προγράμματα με βάση στόχους, εμπειρία, διαθέσιμο εξοπλισμό και δεδομένα δραστηριότητας. Παρακολούθηση σε πραγματικό χρόνο Τα smartwatches και οι αισθητήρες καταγράφουν καρδιακή συχνότητα, βήματα, ύπνο και άλλους δείκτες, με διαφορετικά επίπεδα ακρίβειας ανά συσκευή και μέτρηση. Προσαρμογή της προπόνησης Τα δεδομένα μπορούν να βοηθήσουν στην τροποποίηση της έντασης και του όγκου προπόνησης, εφόσον ερμηνεύονται σωστά. Πρόσβαση από όπου κι αν βρισκόμαστε Εφαρμογές και ψηφιακοί προπονητές επιτρέπουν στον ασκούμενο να προπονείται χωρίς να βρίσκεται υποχρεωτικά σε γυμναστήριο Η ουσιαστική διαφορά είναι ότι παλαιότερα ο ασκούμενος βασιζόταν κυρίως στο πρόγραμμα και στην παρατήρηση του προπονητή. Σήμερα, μπορεί να προστίθεται ένα συνεχές ρεύμα δεδομένων. Αυτό δεν σημαίνει αυτομάτως καλύτερη προπόνηση. Σημαίνει περισσότερες πληροφορίες, οι οποίες χρειάζονται αξιολόγηση. Η ψηφιακή καθοδήγηση μπορεί να βοηθήσει κάποιον να κινηθεί περισσότερο, αλλά δεν έχει αποδειχθεί ότι η χρήση AI από μόνη της εξασφαλίζει σταθερή συνέπεια, καλύτερη τεχνική ή ανώτερα αποτελέσματα προπόνησης . Επομένως, χρειάζεται να διαχωρίζουμε τρία πράγματα: Την ικανότητα της AI να δημιουργεί ένα πρόγραμμα. Την ικανότητά της να προσαρμόζει το πρόγραμμα με βάση αξιόπιστα δεδομένα. Την αποδεδειγμένη βελτίωση της φυσικής κατάστασης και της υγείας του ασκούμενου. Το πρώτο είναι ήδη ευρέως διαθέσιμο. Το δεύτερο εξαρτάται από την ποιότητα των δεδομένων και του συστήματος. Το τρίτο απαιτεί επιστημονική αξιολόγηση και δεν πρέπει να θεωρείται δεδομένο. Τι αλλάζει στον ρόλο του personal trainer; Τα εργαλεία AI μειώνουν τον χρόνο που απαιτείται για ορισμένες εργασίες, όπως η δημιουργία ενός αρχικού προγράμματος, η οργάνωση των προπονήσεων και η καταγραφή της προόδου. Αυτό αλλάζει την αξία που προσφέρει ο επαγγελματίας. Η απλή παράδοση ενός προγράμματος γίνεται πιο εύκολα να αυτοματοποιηθεί. Αντίθετα, η αξιολόγηση του ασκούμενου, η παρατήρηση της κίνησης, η προσαρμογή στην πραγματική του κατάσταση και η ανθρώπινη επικοινωνία αποκτούν ιδιαίτερη σημασία. Η AI μπορεί να βοηθήσει στη δημιουργία προγραμμάτων, στην καταγραφή των επιδόσεων, στην ανάλυση δεδομένων και στην πρόταση τροποποιήσεων της προπόνησης. Ωστόσο, ο επαγγελματίας είναι εκείνος που πρέπει να αξιολογεί αν το πρόγραμμα είναι κατάλληλο για τον συγκεκριμένο ασκούμενο, αν η πρόοδος είναι πραγματική και λειτουργικά σημαντική, αν τα δεδομένα είναι αξιόπιστα και αν οι προτεινόμενες αλλαγές είναι ασφαλείς και επιστημονικά δικαιολογημένες. Παράλληλα, η ανθρώπινη επικοινωνία, η παρακίνηση και η κατανόηση των δυσκολιών που επηρεάζουν τη συνέπεια του ασκούμενου παραμένουν ουσιαστικά στοιχεία της προπονητικής διαδικασίας. Αυτή η διάκριση είναι ιδιαίτερα σημαντική στην αποκατάσταση και στην άσκηση ατόμων με χρόνιες παθήσεις , περιορισμούς κινητικότητας ή αυξημένο κίνδυνο πτώσεων. Ένα γενικό πρόγραμμα δεν υποκαθιστά την εξατομικευμένη προπόνηση και αξιολόγηση. Τι κινδυνεύει να χαθεί; Το σημαντικότερο ζήτημα δεν είναι η ίδια η τεχνολογία, αλλά η άκριτη χρήση της. Η ποιότητα της κίνησης Ένα πρόγραμμα μπορεί να είναι σωστά δομημένο στα χαρτιά, αλλά να μην ανταποκρίνεται στην κινητική ικανότητα του ασκούμενου. Η ορθή επιλογή άσκησης απαιτεί αξιολόγηση, όχι μόνο παραγωγή οδηγιών. Η αυτογνωσία του σώματος Αν ο ασκούμενος βασίζεται αποκλειστικά σε αριθμούς, μπορεί να παραμερίζει την κόπωση, τον πόνο, τη δυσκολία ή την ανάγκη τροποποίησης μιας άσκησης. Οι μετρήσεις είναι χρήσιμες, αλλά δεν αποτελούν πλήρη εικόνα της φυσικής κατάστασης. Η ανθρώπινη επαφή Η σχέση με τον προπονητή, η ενθάρρυνση, η κοινωνική σύνδεση και η προσαρμογή στις πραγματικές συνθήκες της ζωής δεν εξασφαλίζονται από έναν αλγόριθμο. Δεν έχει αποδειχθεί ότι κάθε ψηφιακή παρέμβαση υποκαθιστά εξίσου αποτελεσματικά την ανθρώπινη καθοδήγηση. Η κριτική σκέψη του επαγγελματία Όταν ο προπονητής αποδέχεται άκριτα τις προτάσεις της AI, υπάρχει κίνδυνος να μετατραπεί από αξιολογητή σε απλό εκτελεστή οδηγιών. Υπάρχει και το ζήτημα των προσωπικών δεδομένων. Οι πληροφορίες για την υγεία, τον ύπνο και τη φυσική δραστηριότητα χρειάζονται υπεύθυνη διαχείριση και προστασία. Η επιστημονική τεκμηρίωση δεν επιτρέπει να ισχυριστούμε ότι αυτές οι απώλειες συμβαίνουν αναγκαστικά σε όλους τους χρήστες. Πρόκειται για ουσιαστικούς κινδύνους που πρέπει να λαμβάνονται υπόψη κατά την εφαρμογή της τεχνολογίας. Ποιο είναι το μέλλον της γυμναστικής; Προπόνηση με συνεχή προσαρμογή Τα δεδομένα από αισθητήρες, την προπόνηση και την αποκατάσταση θα μπορούν να χρησιμοποιούνται για πιο εξατομικευμένες προτάσεις. Η πρόκληση θα είναι να αποδειχθεί ότι αυτές οι προσαρμογές βελτιώνουν τα αποτελέσματα και δεν βασίζονται σε παραπλανητικές ενδείξεις. Συνδυασμός AI και ανθρώπινης επίβλεψης Η τεχνολογία θα αναλαμβάνει όλο και περισσότερες εργασίες καταγραφής και υποστήριξης. Ο επαγγελματίας θα χρειάζεται να ερμηνεύει τα αποτελέσματα, να ελέγχει την ποιότητα της κίνησης και να αποφασίζει πότε μια πρόταση δεν είναι κατάλληλη. Περισσότερη εξειδίκευση Η άσκηση για μεγαλύτερες ηλικίες , η λειτουργική προπόνηση, η πρόληψη πτώσεων και η άσκηση για άτομα με χρόνιες παθήσεις απαιτούν εξατομίκευση και επαγγελματική κρίση. Η AI μπορεί να υποστηρίξει αυτές τις υπηρεσίες, χωρίς να υποκαθιστά την αναγκαία κλινική αξιολόγηση. Αλλαγή του επιχειρηματικού μοντέλου Οι υπηρεσίες που βασίζονται μόνο στην παράδοση προγραμμάτων θα αντιμετωπίζουν μεγαλύτερο ανταγωνισμό από ψηφιακά εργαλεία. Η προσωπική επίβλεψη, η εξειδίκευση, η κοινότητα και η ποιότητα της εμπειρίας αποτελούν διαφορετικές υπηρεσίες, τις οποίες η απλή παραγωγή ενός προγράμματος δεν μπορεί από μόνη της να αναπαράγει. Τι δεν αλλάζει, παρά την τεχνολογία Η βιολογία του ανθρώπινου σώματος δεν αλλάζει επειδή εξελίχθηκε το λογισμικό. Η προοδευτική επιβάρυνση, η συνέπεια, η κατάλληλη αποκατάσταση και η προσαρμογή στις δυνατότητες του ατόμου εξακολουθούν να αποτελούν βασικές αρχές της προπόνησης. Οι αλγόριθμοι της AI μπορεί να υποστηρίξουν την εφαρμογή τους. Δεν καταργεί την ανάγκη να εφαρμόζονται σωστά. Το μέλλον δεν θα κριθεί από το ποιος μπορεί να δημιουργήσει τις περισσότερες ασκήσεις, αλλά από το ποιος μπορεί να αξιολογήσει σωστά τον άνθρωπο, να επιλέξει την κατάλληλη παρέμβαση και να αποδείξει ότι αυτή έχει αποτέλεσμα. Η τεχνολογία μπορεί να κάνει τον προπονητή πιο αποτελεσματικό. Η επιστημονική γνώση, η επαγγελματική κρίση και η ανθρώπινη ευθύνη είναι εκείνες που καθορίζουν αν αυτή η δυνατότητα θα αξιοποιηθεί σωστά. Η Σοφία Περδίκη είναι personal trainer και certified Pilates Instructor με ιδιαίτερη εμπειρία στην εκγύμναση ασκουμένων με νευροκινητικά προβλήματα. Είναι απόφοιτος του ΤΕΦΑΑ Αριστοτέλειου Πανεπιστημίου Θεσσαλονίκης και της Σχολής AF Studies. Έχει εργαστεί για περισσότερο από δεκαπέντε χρόνια ως γυμνάστρια σε σχολεία και εκπαιδευτήρια πρωτοβάθμιας και δευτεροβάθμιας εκπαίδευσης ενώ το 2008 δημιούργησε το στούντιο φυσικής αγωγής και ειδικών γυμναστικών που προσφέρει εξειδικευμένα προγράμματα άσκησης, προγράμματα pilates, pilates reformer και ολοκληρωμένα προγράμματα fitness πάντοτε με προσωπική επίβλεψη από την ίδια ή τους συνεργάτες της. items.title: Η ανοικοδόμηση τζαμιών φέρνει κοντά Σιχ, Ινδουιστές και Μουσουλμάνους μετά τη βία στο Παντζάμπ

items.descriptionOriginal: Όλο τον ασφαλιστικό τους φάκελο μπορούν να έχουν από σήμερα οι πολίτες, κατεβάζοντας το νέο ψηφιακό εργαλείο myEOPYY app στο οποίο μπορούν να παρακολουθούν κάθε υπηρεσία που δέχονται μέσω του Εθνικού Οργανισμού Παροχής Υπηρεσιών Υγείας (ΕΟΠΥΥ) . Υποβολή δικαιολογητικών για εκκαθάριση και πληρωμή, παρακολούθηση αποζημιώσεων, προγραμματισμό για ραντεβού στα φαρμακεία του ΕΟΠΥΥ και έκδοση ηλεκτρονικού εισιτηρίου με δυνατότητα παρακολούθησης της αναμονής και της ουράς που τυχόν έχει το φαρμακείο. Αυτές είναι κάποιες από τις υπηρεσίες που θα έχουν άμεσα διαθέσιμες οι ασφαλισμένοι, παράλληλα με οποιαδήποτε υπηρεσία δέχονται από γιατρούς, διαγνωστικά , κέντρα υγείας, δημόσια και ιδιωτικά νοσοκομεία. Η παρουσίαση της νέας εφαρμογής έγινε σε Συνέντευξη Τύπου που πραγματοποιήθηκε στο Υπουργείο Υγείας . Σύμφωνα με όσα ανέφερε ο Υπουργός Υγείας, Άδωνις Γεωργιάδης , από σήμερα η εφαρμογή είναι διαθέσιμη σε τηλέφωνα android και από αύριο σε apple. Παράλληλα με το myEOPYY app , ξεκινά και αξιολόγηση από τους πολίτες για όλους τους παρόχους του ΕΟΠΥΥ. Η αξιολόγηση, στο πρότυπο εκείνης που ήδη γίνεται για τα δημόσια νοσοκομεία μετά το εξιτήριό τους, θα αφορά σε κάθε πάροχο υγείας, δηλαδή κέντρα υγείας, ιδιωτικά νοσοκομεία, διαγνωστικά κέντρα, ιδιώτες γιατρούς. Όπως αναφέρθηκε στη σχετική παρουσίαση, θα ξεκινήσει πιλοτικά με τρεις κατηγορίες παρόχων: Γιατρούς ειδικοτήτων, διαγνωστικά εργαστήρια και φυσικοθεραπευτήρια. Σύμφωνα με τον Υπουργό Υγείας, το νέο app αυτό έρχεται να συμπληρώσει το myhealth app που περιλαμβάνει όλα τα ιατρικά δεδομένα των πολιτών. Στη νέα εφαρμογή θα είναι στο κινητό συγκεντρωμένα όλα τα ασφαλιστικά δεδομένα. Διαφάνεια, έλεγχος και ποιότητα είναι τα τρία στοιχεία που σημείωσε η Αναπληρώτρια Υπουργός Υγείας, Ειρήνη Αγαπηδάκη , σε σχέση με τη νέα δυνατότητα. «Οι ασφαλισμένοι παραπονιούνται για χρεώσεις που δεν θα έπρεπε να έχουν, έτσι πλέον θα έχουν άμεση ενημέρωση» , ανέφερε, προσθέτοντας ότι είναι εξίσου σημαντικό και για την ηγεσία του Υπουργείου Υγείας να λαμβάνει τέτοιου είδους πληροφορία. Τον διοικητή του ΕΟΠΥΥ, Αθανάσιο Ζαμάνη , για την άμεση ανταπόκριση συνεχάρη ο Υφυπουργός Υγείας, Μάριος Θεμιστοκλέους . «Οτιδήποτε δίνει περισσότερα όπλα στους πολίτες, πιο εύκολη και αξιόπιστη ενημέρωση είναι κάτι που μας βοηθά να γινόμαστε καλύτεροι» , σημείωσε. Από την πλευρά του ο κ. Ζαμάνης, τόνισε πως οι ασφαλισμένοι πλέον μπορούν να αξιολογούν την υπηρεσία που λαμβάνουν από κάθε πάροχο. Ειδήσεις σήμερα Συναγερμός για 4 ανθεκτικά «υπερμικρόβια» – Ποιος μύκητας έχει «καταλάβει» τα ελληνικά νοσοκομεία «Άσκηση σημαίνει ζωή»: Το μήνυμα του Υπουργείου Υγείας για την πρόληψη της παχυσαρκίας Μειώνεται ο ΦΠΑ στα προϊόντα περιόδου – Εξετάζεται δωρεάν διάθεση σε σχολεία

items.descriptionOriginal: A money plant is one of the easiest houseplants to grow . It can grow in a glass jar of water, adding a touch of green to a windowsill, desk, or living room. However, yellowing leaves, rotting stems, and slow growth can leave many plant lovers wondering what they are doing wrong. Dipalee Katre, a plant styling enthusiast from New Delhi, shares simple gardening advice on her Instagram page, 'Wabi Sabi with Dipalee' , where she offers tips on growing plants and creating peaceful green spaces at home . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Wabi Sabi with Dipalee | Plant Styling (@dipalee_katre) In one of her videos, she shares three easy tips to help money plants grow better in water. 1. Cut the stem just below a node When taking a cutting from a money plant , pay attention to the node. This is the point on the stem where leaves and roots can appear. She recommends cutting just below a node when preparing a cutting for propagation. Choosing a healthy stem with at least one node gives the cutting a better chance of developing roots and growing into a new plant. 2. Change the water every week Water that sits in a container for too long can accumulate debris and become unsuitable for healthy root growth. Dipalee advises changing the water at least once a week. Fresh water helps keep the roots clean and reduces the build-up of stagnant water. While changing it, check the roots and stems for any signs of rotting. A clean container also helps maintain a healthier growing environment. 3. Add clean stones or pebbles The third tip is to add clean stones or pebbles to the container. These provide support to the cutting, helping it remain upright instead of shifting around in the water. Make sure the stones are clean before adding them. Avoid packing the container too tightly, as the roots need room to grow. With the right cutting, regular water changes, and a little support from pebbles , growing a money plant in water can be an easier way to bring greenery into your home. As Dipalee suggests, try these tips with your own plant and observe how it responds. After all, a few small changes to your gardening routine can make caring for your indoor plants much easier.

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.

items.descriptionOriginal: Το απόλυτο… φιάσκο με έναν 51χρονο αστυνομικό, που υπηρετεί στο Α.Τ. Ραφήνας – Πικερμίου, σημειώθηκε το μεσημέρι της Δευτέρας στην Παλλήνη. Λίγο πριν πιάσει υπηρεσία φύλαξης σε στατικό στόχο, πέρασε από το Αστυνομικό Τμήμα και παρέλαβε τον εξοπλισμό του: ένα υποπολυβόλο MP-5, έναν ασύρματο και μία χειροβομβίδα κρότου-λάμψης. Τα έβαλε, σύμφωνα με πληροφορίες, σε μία σακούλα και ανέβηκε στη μοτοσικλέτα του για να πάει στο σημείο όπου θα εκτελούσε υπηρεσία. Κατά τη διάρκεια της διαδρομής, στην περιοχή της Παλλήνης, η σακούλα σκίστηκε και ο οπλισμός έπεσε στον δρόμο! Ο αστυνομικός, όταν το κατάλαβε, γύρισε πίσω και άρχισε να ψάχνει. Βρήκε τον ασύρματο και τη χειροβομβίδα. Το MP-5 όμως… άφαντο. Επικράτησε πανικός και έρευνα, ενώ ο 51χρονος συνελήφθη για παράβαση του νόμου περί όπλων και για μη ασφαλή φύλαξη οπλισμού. Με προφορική εντολή εισαγγελέα αφέθηκε ελεύθερος, ενώ τη δικογραφία σχηματίζει το Τμήμα Δίωξης και Εξιχνίασης Εγκλημάτων Ραφήνας – Πικερμίου το οποίο ερευνά και πού κατέληξε το υποπολυβόλο.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action Reading Time: 3 minutes Wildlife conservation filmmaking connects audiences with wild places and the people protecting them. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives viewers a reason to care about wild places they may never see in person. Fin and Fur Films , an award-winning production company, builds its work around that idea. Its team focuses on wildlife, adventure, and conservation stories. The company says it is proudest of films that led to real-world conservation impacts. That goal shapes every project. In wildlife conservation filmmaking, a film succeeds when it moves audiences to care, not just when it entertains. Ben Masters, founder and director, started the company in 2012 with a Kickstarter campaign. Kickstarter is an online fundraising platform where many people donate small amounts. That campaign paid for the film Unbranded. Unbranded follows four young cowboys who adopted, trained, and rode a string of wild mustangs 3,000 miles from Mexico to Canada. That is about the distance across the continental United States. The route crossed some of the wildest terrain in the American West. The trip included runaway horses, a sassy donkey, perilous mountain passes, and rodeos. It also brought sickness, injury, and death. The film won the Audience Award at Telluride Mountainfilm and the Hot Docs Film Festival. Unbranded also shines a light on the complex situation facing the country’s wild horses. The adventure holds attention, and the film explains the issue along the way. Wildlife conservation filmmaking often works this way. The River and the Wall takes a similar approach. Five friends travel 1,200 miles from El Paso to the Gulf of Mexico through the unknown wilds of the Texas borderlands. They go by horse, mountain bike, and canoe. That distance equals nearly a full day of nonstop highway driving, but the friends covered it much more slowly. They set out to document the borderlands. They also wanted to explore how a border wall could affect the natural environment. As the wilderness gave way to the more populated Lower Rio Grande Valley, the friends met the human side of the immigration debate. The trip took an emotional turn they had not planned for. Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story brings wildlife conservation filmmaking to an entire state. Actor Matthew McConaughey narrates the visually stunning film. It celebrates Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Wildlife conservation filmmaking comes to an entire state in Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story , narrated by Matthew McConaughey, a visually stunning film celebrating Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Photo courtesy of Fin and Fur Films . The film aims to protect the state’s remaining wild places. It shows how water and wildlife depend on each other. It also recognizes Texas’s important role in conservation across the continent. Reach matters in wildlife conservation filmmaking. Fin and Fur Films has shared its work through Netflix, Apple TV, PBS Nature, Prime, National Geographic, and LoveNature. The films have also appeared in large theatrical releases and on international television. Global Wildlife Conservation notes that well-made environmental documentaries can bring people closer to nature and inspire them to protect it. The Fin and Fur Films catalog shows how that works in practice. Each story pairs a real adventure with a real conservation question. Partnerships help wildlife conservation filmmaking go further. The company has worked with American Rivers, The Nature Conservancy, and Texan by Nature. It has also partnered with brands such as H-E-B and YETI. The numbers show how far a small team can stretch. The company has produced five feature films and more than 30 short films. It has worked with more than 40 conservation groups, which is roughly one partner group per film. See also: A Documentary About Overfishing Sparked Blue Marine Foundation’s Ocean Conservation Mission Masters says the crew keeps its roots as river lovers, backcountry horsemen, and field-savvy wildlife biologists. He also stresses that each film is a team effort. Dozens, or even hundreds, of people contribute to each one. Masters credits partners, collaborators, donors, contractors, and the viewers who give their time to watch. That shared support keeps the work going. Audiences are part of the effort, too. Good stories make conservation feel personal. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives those stories a wide audience. Which wild place would you most like to see protected next? The post How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns
items.description: Χρόνος ανάγνωσης: 3 λεπτά Ο Yuvelis Morales Blanco κέρδισε το Περιβαλλοντικό Βραβείο Goldman 2026 για τη διακοπή του fracking στις κοινότητες του ποταμού Magdalena της Κολομβίας και τη συμβολή στη διακοπή του δρόμου και την εξασφάλιση δύο πιλοτικών έργων με το βραβείο Goldman Eco News. Ένα πανεπιστήμιο…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns Reading Time: 3 minutes Yuvelis Morales Blanco won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and helping halt two pilot projects and secure a landmark court ruling. A university student began stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns by knocking on her neighbors’ doors. Seven years later, Yuvelis Morales Blanco has won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for that work. The prize honors grassroots environmental leaders from six world regions each year. Her campaign helped stop two pilot fracking projects near her hometown of Puerto Wilches. It also led to a Constitutional Court ruling that upheld her Afro-Colombian community’s right to a say. To date, no fracking project has moved forward anywhere in Colombia. Morales Blanco, now 24, grew up in a family of subsistence fishers on the Magdalena River. The river flows nearly 1,000 miles from the Andes to the Caribbean, about the distance from Boston to Atlanta. For the roughly 30,000 people of Puerto Wilches, it provides food, income, and identity. The town also sits in the heart of Colombia’s oil country. Ecopetrol, the largest and majority state-owned oil company, is based in nearby Barrancabermeja. Between 2015 and 2022, about 40% of its more than 2,000 oil spills happened in this region. That works out to roughly two spills a week for eight years. In 2018, a leak at the Lizama 158 well displaced about 100 families and killed thousands of fish. So when the government proposed fracking nearby, residents had reason to worry. In 2019, then-President Iván Duque announced two pilot projects called Kalé and Platero. Ecopetrol led both, with ExxonMobil as operator and majority partner on Platero. Fracking, short for hydraulic fracturing, pumps water, sand, and chemicals into rock at high pressure. The pressure cracks the rock and frees trapped oil or gas. The process uses large amounts of water and can contaminate rivers and groundwater. Morales Blanco was studying environmental engineering at the time. She paused her degree and began visiting neighbors to explain the risks. She also joined the Alianza Colombia Libre de Fracking, or Colombia Free from Fracking Alliance. With the alliance, she helped lead protests outside the Ecopetrol refinery. In January 2022, she testified at permit hearings and organized a peaceful sit-in. Soon after the sit-in, armed men showed up at her home. She fled Colombia, and France granted her asylum in February 2022. No one has been convicted for the threats against her. Exile in France did not end her campaign. She received the Marianne Initiative award for human rights defenders and raised the issue with President Emmanuel Macron. She also brought the case before the International Rights of Nature Tribunal. Back home, the campaign for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns began winning in court. In April 2022, a court suspended environmental permits for both projects until companies consulted local communities. Months later, newly elected President Gustavo Petro announced his opposition to fracking. Community organizing helped secure a court-ordered suspension of two fracking projects in 2022, a key step in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River, followed months later by President Gustavo Petro’s opposition to fracking. Photo by Christian Escobar Mora courtesy of Goldman Environmental Prize . Ecopetrol suspended the project contracts in September 2022. By November, it had halted Kalé and Platero and undone its agreements with ExxonMobil. The decisive ruling came in August 2024. Colombia’s Constitutional Court found that the pilots violated the community’s right to free, prior, and informed consent. Under this principle, companies must consult communities and win their agreement before projects affect their land. That decision reaches beyond Puerto Wilches. It confirms that Afro-Colombian communities have a legal voice over what happens on their territory. The precedent matters for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and anywhere similar projects appear. Morales Blanco has since returned to Puerto Wilches and keeps organizing with the alliance. She describes the Magdalena as the life that sustains her family and her fishing community. She also points out that her region produces great energy wealth while many residents stay poor. The Global Greengrants Fund, which supports the alliance, notes that each prize winner represents a broader movement. More than 80 of the fund’s partners and allies have received the prize since 1993. Afro-Colombian fishing communities stood beside her in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns. Morales Blanco won for the South and Central America region, one of six 2026 winners , all of whom were women. The others came from Nigeria, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Papua New Guinea, and the United States. Colombia’s politics have shifted since her win. President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August 2026 after campaigning to expand fracking. Still, the 2024 ruling gives communities like Puerto Wilches firm legal ground to demand a say. Stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities didn’t require a big budget or political office. It took a young woman who knew her river and kept going after threats forced her abroad. Her prize shows how local action can shape national policy. The post Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Το 2017, ηγήθηκε μιας διεπιστημονικής ομάδας σε ένα h…
items.descriptionOriginal: Behind some of India's biggest medical milestones was a doctor who dedicated his life to making advanced healthcare accessible. Padma Shri awardee and eminent neurosurgeon Dr Ashok Kumar Mahapatra passed away at AIIMS Delhi on Monday evening, leaving behind a remarkable four-decade career in medicine. In 2017, he led a multidisciplinary team in a historic 16-hour surgery to separate Odisha's conjoined twins, Jaga and Kalia. Both children survived, marking a landmark moment in Indian neurosurgery. Yet, his contribution extended far beyond the operating theatre. As the founding director of AIIMS Bhubaneswar (2012–2016), he built the institution from the ground up, introducing medical, nursing and super-speciality courses. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he continued serving public healthcare by overseeing the creation of over 2,600 dedicated beds across Odisha. An accomplished academic, he also authored around 870 research papers and 16 books, advancing medical knowledge across generations. Conferred the Padma Shri in 2025, Dr Mahapatra leaves behind a lasting impact through the lives he saved, the institutions he built, and the doctors he inspired. Rest in peace, Dr Mahapatra. #DrAshokMahapatra #PadmaShri #IndianHealthcare #IndianDoctors #AIIMSBhubaneswar

Αυτή η ήσυχη στιγμή βρίσκεται στο επίκεντρο του δεκαετούς έργου της Ursula Kermer, Mehr ist Mehr ("More is More"), ένα δίκτυο εθελοντών που μετατρέπει μεμονωμένα τετράγωνα νήματος σε κουβέρτες, μπολερό και κουβέρτες.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A small knitted tube — open at both ends, just wide enough for two hands — and a child with anxiety found each other in an Austrian classroom. That quiet moment is at the heart of Ursula Kermer's decade-long project, Mehr ist Mehr ("More is More"), a volunteer network that turns individual squares of yarn into blankets, boleros, and twiddle muffs for people moving through hard seasons of life. Kermer, an art therapist, is honest about what the project cannot do: "Our project does not solve problems; it does not make crisis go away." But it is constant, and that constancy — the weekly knitting circles, the puzzling together of mismatched squares, the packages of wool arriving unbidden from strangers — turns out to be its own kind of medicine. The blankets travel to families whose children have cancer, to people who cannot pay their heating bills, to rehabilitation centers where a counselor leaves them draped over chairs so that someone in crisis might simply reach out and choose one. Most knitters never know whose hands will eventually hold their work, and Kermer photographs every step so they know where it ends — just not with whom. She describes the whole endeavor as resilience training in disguise: choosing a color, trusting a process, watching mismatched pieces become something whole. For her, the image that holds it all is a network — "growing and moving, and provides a resilient safety" — as easily overlooked, but just as strong as the individual threads that compose spools of yarn.

items.title: Πώς ένα αυτοσχέδιο μαξιλάρι με χαρτομάντιλα και ιατρικές ταινίες βοήθησε αυτόν τον ορειβάτη στα 16000 πόδια πάνω από την επιφάνεια της θάλασσας

items.description: Φανταστείτε να φτάσετε σε μια ορεινή κατασκήνωση 16.000 πόδια πάνω από την επιφάνεια της θάλασσας, μόνο για να συνειδητοποιήσετε ότι η περίοδός σας έχει ξεκινήσει και δεν έχετε σερβιέτες. items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine reaching a mountain camp 16,000 feet above sea level, only to realise that your period has started and you have no sanitary pads . There is no nearby shop, no easy way to restock supplies and no one around to ask for help. With another four to five days left at the location, what do you do? For mountaineer Yogeshwari Bohare, the answer was to work with what she had. Bohare's makeshift pad , made with tissue paper and medical tape which is now going viral, has brought attention to a practical question: are menstrual hygiene needs adequately covered in expedition safety plans? In a video shared on Instagram, Bohare explained that her period had started the previous night. With sanitary pads unavailable and no other women around, she decided to improvise using tissue paper and medical tape. She layered the tissue to make it thicker, folded it and used the tape to secure the edges. Once she had assembled the makeshift pad, she held it up to the camera and said, "Let's see if this works or not." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mountaineer Yogeshwari (@yogi_on_everest) Climbers prepare for changing weather, difficult terrain, injuries and altitude-related illness. But menstruation does not follow an expedition schedule, and access to essential menstrual products can become difficult when a team is far from the nearest settlement. Bohare summed up what the mountains had taught her in her Instagram caption: "Mountains teach you more than climbing; they teach you how to adapt, survive, and find solutions when things get tough." She also pointed out that periods do not pause for expeditions, even though the challenges women face in the mountains are rarely discussed. But what does India's mountaineering safety framework say about women's menstrual health? What happens when periods meet the mountains? For women on multi-day expeditions, menstrual hygiene involves more than packing enough sanitary pads. Climbers may also need access to clean water, privacy to change, appropriate waste-disposal arrangements and a way to carry used products back from environmentally sensitive mountain areas. At high altitudes, these practical requirements must be considered alongside the usual demands of an expedition . A climber cannot necessarily leave the group to find a shop or wait until the next day to obtain supplies. She also pointed out that periods do not pause for expeditions, even though the challenges women face in the mountains are rarely discussed. Photograph: (Mountaineer Yogeshwari) Bohare's video does not establish whether her expedition organisers had a menstrual hygiene plan or whether other arrangements were available. But it highlights why these needs deserve a place in expedition preparation, rather than being left entirely to individual climbers to manage when a period arrives unexpectedly. What do the IMF's safety guidelines say? The Indian Mountaineering Foundation (IMF), the national body responsible for mountaineering activities, has published safety guidelines for expedition operators. Its rules recognise that an expedition requires planning beyond the act of climbing itself. The IMF's published advisory does not explicitly list sanitary pads or other menstrual products as mandatory expedition supplies. Nor do they spell out specific requirements for menstrual hygiene facilities or the disposal of used products. A small addition to a big expedition Bohare's experience is a reminder that mountaineering preparation must also account for the people undertaking the climb, not just the terrain they will encounter. The IMF could clarify whether menstrual hygiene is covered in its existing operational guidance and consider adding explicit recommendations for expedition organisers. Operators, too, can make menstrual products part of routine supply planning, alongside first-aid equipment and other essentials . At 16,000 feet, Bohare found a temporary solution with the materials available to her. Her video has made a rarely discussed challenge visible. But menstruation is not an unusual event that should catch women out of place in the outdoors. It is a normal bodily process, and preparing for it should be as ordinary as checking the weather before a climb. Sources: 'Mountaineer Opens Up About Facing Her Period At 16,000 Feet With No Sanitary Pads' : By Astitva Raj, Published on 24 October 2026 Advisory(Precautions & Recommendations) -Indian Mountaineering Foundation
