items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Cofán Rangers Protecting the Amazon Guard 450,000 Hectares of Ecuadorian Rainforest Reading Time: 3 minutes Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon carry 100-pound packs on monthlong patrols, defending ancestral rainforest territory that benefits the entire planet. The Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon have safeguarded the Ecuadorian rainforest for centuries, living where the Amazon Basin rises toward the Andes. Among the region’s oldest surviving indigenous cultures, the Cofán now protect more than one million acres of ancestral territory, roughly the size of the U.S. state of Delaware, containing primary forest, wild rivers, swamplands, and several thousand plant and animal species found nowhere else. That protection intensified after oil exploitation and the colonists who followed threatened to overwhelm Cofán lands. In response, Cofán leadership founded Fundación Sobrevivencia Cofán in 1999, an organization built on what its founders described as a fight-for-rights-or-disappear mindset. The Cofán Survival Fund, an independent U.S.-based nonprofit, supports that work by channeling donations directly into Cofán-led conservation programs. At the center of Cofán people’s protection of the Amazon is GuardAmazonas Cofán, formerly known as the Cofán Park Guards. Since 2003, teams of Cofán rangers have delimited, secured, monitored, and protected their homeland, using GPS units and drones to gather intelligence on threats before coordinating with police and the military to counter illegal incursions. The program’s success convinced Ecuador’s Ministry of Environment to more than double the Cofán’s legally recognized ancestral territory. Today, nearly 50 Cofán rangers patrol in five-person teams, carrying full packs on monthlong expeditions that demand extreme physical fitness and deep forest knowledge. Unlike many indigenous territory-protection programs, GuardAmazonas pays its rangers, recognizing that sustained, full-time conservation work demands fair compensation for families bearing real costs and risks. Teams deliberately mix members from different communities and generations, transmitting ecological knowledge across the Cofán homeland while strengthening unified national identity. Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon through GuardAmazonas receive fair pay for sustained, full-time conservation work, with patrol teams deliberately mixing members from different communities and generations to transmit ecological knowledge across the Cofán homeland. Photo courtesy of Cofán Survival Fund . The work of Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon extends well beyond ranger patrols into cultural survival and scientific partnership. Between 2001 and 2008, the foundation coordinated four Rapid Biological Inventories with Chicago Field Museum biologists, leading directly to expanded territorial protection. That collaboration earned a 2013 MacArthur Award for Creative and Effective Institutions. The Charapa Project shows how Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon lead species recovery. Commercial egg harvesting nearly eliminated the Amazonian river turtle from Ecuadorian beaches until Cofán communities began raising hatchlings in protected ponds in the 1980s, dramatically improving survival rates before release. In Zábalo, families now protect most turtle nests they find, and travelers along the Aguarico River encounter river turtles sunning themselves on nearly every log once they enter Cofán territory, a result confirmed by peer-reviewed research co-authored by Cofán community members. Climate change has not spared Cofán lands, prompting the creation of the Lifeboat Garden Project. As scorching temperatures and unpredictable rainfall diminished important food and medicinal plant species, project leaders transplanted them to more ecologically stable upriver land, preserving botanical knowledge for future generations while protecting additional forest in a heavily deforested area. Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon also invest in human capital. The Cofán Higher Education Project sends entire families, not just individual students, to Quito, where parents pursue university degrees while children attend quality schools, preserving language and cultural identity through shared communal housing. The Seguro Campesino Project enrolls Cofán families in Ecuadorian social welfare programs, sends medical brigades to remote communities, and removes financial pressures that might otherwise force compromises on territorial conservation commitments. Innovation among Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon also extends to transportation. After the successful Ecocanoa Project taught Cofán artisans to build durable fiberglass canoes instead of felling endangered trees, the Solar Canoe Project now develops battery-powered alternatives to fossil-fuel motors, creating quieter waterways that benefit wildlife, hunting, fishing, and ecotourism alike. Ecotourism remains central to Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon, tracing back to the 1970s, when FSC founder Randy Borman and Cofán community members began hosting visitors along the Aguarico River and eventually established the community of Zábalo. Rather than staging performances, Cofán guides position themselves as credentialed experts who share ecological knowledge directly, keeping more revenue by controlling ecotourism operations rather than losing profits to outside intermediaries. Felipe Borman, current Executive Director of the foundation and recently elected Director of Territory for the Cofán ethnic federation NOA’IKE, continues work his father Randy began, coordinating fieldwork across the Cofán-Bermejo Ecological Reserve and Río Cofanes Territory. The foundation’s Rapid Response Team stays vigilant over changing laws and policies that threaten Cofán land rights, while accompanying patients through Ecuador’s healthcare system and coordinating visits from scientists, officials, and allies. As climate negotiations worldwide increasingly recognize indigenous stewardship as essential to global conservation outcomes, Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon demonstrate what sustained, community-led territorial defense can achieve. The foundation emphasizes that funding Cofán rangers protects the forest the whole world depends on, not just Cofán communities, positioning indigenous-led conservation as climate infrastructure that benefits everyone far beyond Ecuador’s Amazonian lowlands. The post Cofán Rangers Protecting the Amazon Guard 450,000 Hectares of Ecuadorian Rainforest appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: "I understood that no dish is difficult to make if you are genuinely interested and really want to cook it from your heart." For 20-year-old Visista, that lesson came from a kitchen, not from a classroom. At four, she stood beside her grandmother Lakshmi as she made chapatis for lunch every day . She did not know how to knead the dough or roll it properly. She only knew that she wanted to try. "My grandmother was making chapatis every day for lunch, and I used to see her and wanted to try," she recalls. "So I just joined her." What began as a childhood love for cooking gradually grew into an interest in traditional dishes, especially recipes that people rarely make anymore. Visista began exploring how these dishes were originally prepared, the ingredients they used, and the stories behind them. Over the years, she has documented more than 250 recipes. She shares her work through 'TRUE FOOD', a recipe section on the website of Aikanthika, the farm in central Karnataka where she grew up. Here, she recreates traditional dishes using ingredients and cooking methods passed down through generations, making it possible for others to try these recipes in their own kitchens. Her curiosity about food was nurtured by an unusual upbringing, where she had the freedom to explore whatever interested her. She has never attended a conventional school. She followed Swashikshan (self-directed learning) at Aikanthika, where education was part of daily life rather than something confined to a classroom. She learnt through questions, books, the internet, conversations with her parents, farm life and the freedom to try things herself. "I have liked food and tasting new dishes since childhood. I liked doing the whole process of making a dish myself, from beginning to end, and then eating what I had made," she explains. That instinct to understand something by doing it has stayed with her. Today, when she comes across an old recipe, she wants to know where it came from, why certain ingredients were used, and whether it can still be made. Lessons from a farm, books and everyday life Aikanthika was founded in 1996. Visista lives there as part of the Aikanthika Tribe, helping with the day-to-day life of the farm and events around natural farming and natural living. Before Aikanthika's traditional wood-fired mud cob oven was built around February or March 2017, she mostly made Indian sweets on the stovetop. "My learning process has always been part of daily life rather than something that happened at a fixed time," she says. "I learnt about things that interested me and also things that I felt were necessary to know." If she had a question, she went to her parents. If they knew the answer, they taught her. If they did not, they helped her find it through books or the internet. Her younger brother Varchas (17) grew up in the same environment. He also follows Swashikshan and helps with the farm, natural building, and other activities. "For us, Swashikshan was just normal life," he says. "We learnt by doing things instead of just studying from textbooks." He remembers his sister as a child who hardly ever wanted to remain a spectator. "She was always keen to learn and liked trying things herself. She would experiment and find her own way instead of following what someone told her," he says. For Visista, the kitchen became one of her favourite places to put that curiosity into practice. From her grandmother's chapatis to baking in a mud oven Visista's earliest cooking memories are tied to her mother Kruthii and grandmother, who were regularly in the kitchen. "I think what drew me to the kitchen was the joy of putting ingredients together and watching them become something delicious," she tells The Better India . "There is a particular satisfaction in it that is difficult to put into words. And when my family eats what I have made and tells me how much they liked it, that gives me another level of happiness." At seven, she began baking. Before Aikanthika's traditional wood-fired mud cob oven was built around February or March 2017, she mostly made Indian sweets on the stovetop and occasionally baked a cake there. The new oven opened up more possibilities. She began making cakes, cookies, muffins, and other baked dishes, though she remained more focused on stovetop cooking until around 2020. Her habit of looking beyond the recipe itself began in 2018. She started researching old, traditional, and forgotten recipes from India and around the world, many of which had nothing to do with baking. By 2020, she was also tracing the stories and origins behind the dishes she made. This research gradually drew her towards traditional baking, especially as she began reading about sourdough and older baking methods. "I became more interested in history and wanted to understand where our food traditions came from. That interest took me down a whole new path of learning," she says. At the farm, the family does not use ingredients such as white flour, refined sugar, bottled sauces, flavourings and packaged ready-to-use ingredients. Instead of trying to remake every modern recipe without them, she began looking for recipes that existed before these ingredients became common. "I became interested in cooking the dishes that most people don't cook anymore," she says. "I especially enjoy cooking traditional dishes that have longer processes and take more time to make." How an old recipe becomes part of her collection As she continued experimenting with recipes, she began documenting the ones that worked in a book. Eventually, she and her father, Raghava, thought it would be meaningful to share this collection more widely, which led to TRUE FOOD. The idea was to create a place where people could find recipes made with traditional ingredients and methods. "That vision has not really changed," she confirms. Some of the recipes are also part of her family's own food traditions, passed down to her by her mother and grandmother. When the family travels to rural areas, tribal villages, or other people's homes, Visista pays attention to what is being cooked. If she tastes something special, she asks for the recipe and writes it down. Visitors and global volunteers at the farm have also shared recipes with her. By 2020, she was also tracing the stories and origins behind the dishes she made. If she knows the name of a dish but does not have its recipe, she searches online. She prefers recipes written by people from the region where the dish originated, as she feels they are more likely to reflect its traditional preparation. She also turns to digital research to trace a dish's history and understand which ingredients may have been used when it first originated, helping her assess how closely a recipe reflects its traditional form. Once she finds a recipe, she checks whether its ingredients are available in her region and whether they fit with the principles followed at Aikanthika. If something is unavailable or unsuitable, she looks for the closest appropriate substitute. "I usually cook a recipe once before documenting it, and while making it and tasting the final dish, I pay attention to the overall result, especially the taste, texture, and whether it feels right as a whole," she says. If something feels wrong, she makes it again and adjusts it. Her mother, grandmother, and other family members taste what she makes and offer feedback before she documents it on TRUE FOOD. Giving pizza & street food a traditional twist She uses freshly milled whole grains, jaggery, unrefined oils, eggs from indigenous chicken breeds, and farm produce instead of refined flour, white sugar, and preservatives. "For me, using traditional ingredients is important because I have found that they bring much more taste and nutritional value to the food," she says. "When I make the same dish using healthy traditional ingredients instead of highly refined and processed ones, I find that the food is not only more nourishing but also much more delicious." That approach extends to familiar favourites like pizza and street food, which she also enjoys making at home. "We do eat these kinds of dishes, but when we make them ourselves using ingredients from our farm, and source what we don't grow from organic or natural farmers, they can become much healthier while still being delicious," she says. Varchas has seen this approach firsthand. "She takes foods we usually enjoy outside and recreates them at home using fresh, natural ingredients instead of processed ones," he says. "And somehow, she manages to make them taste even better." His own contribution is usually tasting. "Honestly, my main job is tasting. I really love her cooking, so whenever she experiments with something new, I am always happy to be the first one to try it," he says. He also helps light the fire in the cob oven. The recipes that taught her to keep trying Sourdough is one of the recipes that remains particularly special to Visista. Being able to bake bread and pizza using traditional and original methods was memorable for her. Jolada rotti (a sorghum flatbread from Karnataka) gave her another valuable lesson. "I grew up hearing people say that it was difficult to roll, so I also thought it would be hard to make," she says. "But when I actually made it myself with my mother about five years ago, we not only successfully made it, but I also understood that no dish is difficult to make if you are genuinely interested and really want to cook it." Eventually, she and her father, Raghava, thought it would be meaningful to share this collection more widely, which led to TRUE FOOD. For Varchas, that willingness to experiment is what defines her approach. "She usually researches a recipe first, then tries making it and sees how it turns out. If something does not work, she looks at what went wrong, makes changes, and tries again. Sometimes it takes a few attempts to get it right," he says. That is also how she approaches learning outside the kitchen. Helping people cook traditional dishes again Volunteers and visitors from India and abroad experience Aikanthika's traditional ingredients and cooking methods , including the cob oven. "When we share these recipes with people who visit the farm, they are usually fascinated because many of these are new to them," Varchas says. "They get to see and try traditional ways of baking that they may not have come across before." People who have tried TRUE FOOD recipes have also written to Visista about their experiences. "Hearing that people are actually making these dishes at home and liking the results makes me feel that the work is reaching people and making an impact," she says. For Visista, sharing a recipe means giving someone else the chance to make it in their own kitchen. "I hope people realise that healthy food can also be delicious," she says. "There is a common idea that healthy food is not very interesting or tasty to eat, and I want to show that it doesn't have to be that way. I hope that the traditional recipes I document will continue to be cooked and will not be forgotten." From her grandmother's kitchen to the next recipe The same child who once stood beside Lakshmi to learn how to make chapatis now researches old recipes, studies ingredients, cooks, tastes, and documents what works. Her approach to learning has followed a similar pattern: asking questions, finding answers, trying things out and learning from the results. "When I am genuinely interested in something, I can learn and do much more than I initially thought I could," she says. Her brother has watched that eagerness grow. "I think this way of trying things and learning by doing is a big part of Swashikshan ," he says. She wants to continue in the same way. She plans to research traditional recipes from more regions and cuisines and keep adding them to TRUE FOOD. Volunteers and visitors from India and abroad experience Aikanthika's traditional ingredients and cooking methods, including the cob oven. For someone who never went through a conventional school, her lessons have been everywhere. In her grandmother's kitchen. On the farm. In books and conversations. In an old recipe shared by someone she met on a journey. In an unsuccessful bake that needed another attempt. And in the happiness of watching someone else cook something she had once researched and made herself. At four, she wanted to know how her grandmother made chapatis. At 20, she is trying to make sure that many more old recipes do not disappear from the table. To learn more about Aikanthika, click here . You can also find Visista's recipes in the TRUE FOOD section of the Aikanthika farm website . All pictures courtesy Raghava.

Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Στραβίζοντας μέσα από τα κιάλια μου, σάρωση th…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Stephanie Szarmach , a James Smithson Postdoctoral Fellow at the Smithsonian Institution, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Squinting through my binoculars, I scanned the dense branches of a black spruce, trying my best to catch a glimpse of the thin legs of a small black, white, and yellow songbird. I was on the hunt for a yellow-rumped warbler — a bird affectionately called “butter-butt” by bird-watchers after the distinctive buttery yellow patch of feathers above its tail. Once I spotted a flash of red on one of the bird’s legs, I knew that this individual was special — in fact, it was one that I already knew well. That’s because I had placed identifying bands on it the previous year as part of my Ph.D. research , and it was carrying a very important piece of new technology. Johanna Beam Stephanie Szarmach holds a yellow-rumped warbler that was banded as part of a study. I played the high-pitched “warble ” of its song through a speaker placed below a mist net of fine, nearly invisible mesh. Thinking another male had intruded on his territory, the bird quickly descended. My tactic worked — he got caught in the net. As I gently removed him, I breathed a sigh of relief as I saw the Tic Tac-size device sitting on his back. Over the past year, this warbler carried a multisensor geolocator backpack throughout his migratory journey, recording the long trek from his breeding grounds in Anchorage, Alaska, to a yet unknown winter refuge and back again. Working with my Ph.D. adviser, evolutionary biologist David Toews , I deployed dozens of these cutting-edge tags to illuminate the migratory journeys of these high-latitude breeding warblers at a scale not previously possible for small birds. Stephanie Szarmach A yellow-rumped warbler wears a multisensor geolocator backpack. Now, after a year of waiting, I finally had the data in hand. How Can Scientists Track Small Birds? Researchers began tracking the movements of migrating birds in the late 1960s using radio telemetry , a technique that requires tagged birds to be physically followed with receiver equipment, sometimes aided by a small aircraft. Then, as GPS became more widely available in the early 2000s, satellite tags let researchers accurately track birds remotely. However, GPS transmitters are hefty — even just the battery that powers them is too heavy to be carried by the majority of small migratory songbirds, which often weigh less than a spoonful of sugar. To address this problem, researchers developed ingenious little light-level geolocators . These miniature tags minimize weight by containing only a tiny battery, clock, computer chip, and light sensor. They store data internally rather than transmitting it — hence my need to recapture tagged birds a year later. Researchers infer a bird’s locations from the timing of sunrise and sunset, which vary predictably across the globe and throughout the year. Stephanie Szarmach Each harness loop of the multisensor geolocator goes around one of the bird’s legs and the tag sits on the bird’s lower back. Light-level geolocators have opened new windows into the migrations of small birds , but they also have limitations: Their estimated locations can err by hundreds of miles, and this uncertainty becomes impractically high around the equinoxes, when day length is the same worldwide. More recently, researchers developed a newer method of geolocation that uses atmospheric pressure to circumvent these limitations. When a bird ascends during a migratory flight, a barometric geolocator records a steep drop in air pressure, capturing the timing of departure and arrival for every stop along a bird’s migration route. In between flights, the pressure the tag records reflects the elevation at the bird’s position. Knowing the bird’s elevation helps to narrow down possible locations, which researchers can then refine further by comparing the change in pressure over time recorded by the tag to global weather data using the computer program GeoPressureR . The unique pattern of rises and falls in pressure acts as a kind of pressure fingerprint for a specific location. Including light and wind data in the model of the bird’s movements can increase precision even more. Stephanie Szarmach Atmospheric pressure data collected from a multisensor geolocator carried by a yellow-rumped warbler over five days in spring. When the bird is stationary, such as when resting at a stopover site, the measured pressure remains steady. During migratory flights, when the bird ascends into the sky, the pressure drops and fluctuates dramatically. New Tech Answers an Old Question We used these new multisensor backpacks to study the migration patterns of myrtle warblers , the northern subspecies of yellow-rumped warbler, which breed across North America’s boreal forest. Myrtle warblers in the northeast are known to winter along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, but where northwestern populations migrate has been more of a mystery. In 1899, ornithologist Richard McGregor observed myrtle warblers wintering in coastal California , and hypothesized that these birds might breed in Alaska and British Columbia. Using these new tags allowed us to test whether warblers breeding in Anchorage, Alaska, actually followed the shortest migration route to winter in California. To our surprise — and probably to McGregor’s as well, if he were still alive — we found that all the birds we tracked traveled east across the boreal forest of Canada before shifting south to the Gulf Coast – certainly not the Pacific Coast route we expected. All told, this 6,800-mile (10,900-kilometer) round-trip journey was much longer than we anticipated for a species commonly considered a short- or medium-distance migrant. Figure by Stephanie Szarmach. Warbler illustration by Emily Griffith Researchers tracked the routes six myrtle warblers flew on their fall migration southeast from Anchorage, Alaska. Why Take Such a Circuitous Route? The long, seemingly suboptimal route taken by our Alaskan myrtle warblers is actually mirrored by some other songbird species tracked from northwestern North America, including blackpoll warblers and Swainson’s thrushes . Part of this pattern may relate back to the glaciations that isolated ancient populations of birds millions of years ago. The thinking goes that as these glaciers spread, they squashed the ranges of formerly northern species into the south. Then, as the glaciers slowly receded, the forests gradually reexpanded. As more land opened up, birds moved farther north and west into that habitat. Each season some birds went a little farther as the forest available in their northern breeding grounds expanded. For migratory species such as myrtle warblers, the farther north and west their breeding range expanded, the longer the migration to their southern wintering ground became. Scientists think migration routes are genetically encoded . The birds’ genes may have traced this expansion front, like Hansel and Gretel putting down breadcrumbs as they journeyed deeper and deeper into the forest. Today’s migration routes still trace that incrementally expanded path, even though the glaciers that shaped the original boundaries are long gone. We’re still not sure exactly where the California-wintering myrtle warblers spotted in the 1800s are breeding. We suspect that a small proportion of the Anchorage-breeding birds may migrate to California , but that most of them travel from more distant, unstudied regions of Alaska or Yukon. Future research, potentially tagging myrtle warblers directly on the California wintering grounds, will shed more light on this population and why certain individuals follow a different migration route. Barometric Geolocation Provides New Data Today, this new geolocation approach improves scientists’ ability to study the migrations of small birds and supports more effective conservation actions across the course of the entire year . More precise location estimates help researchers identify key stopover and wintering sites in need of protection and better understand the threats birds face throughout their journeys. These geolocators also reveal the altitude of migratory flights, which is important for understanding the risk of birds colliding with buildings or wind turbines. Because these new tags capture pressure data for every migratory flight, they’re especially valuable for studying migration timing. Researchers have combined data from over 50 bird species to understand at what time of day or night different birds migrate . Now, as a postdoctoral researcher at the Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center , I am integrating multisensor geolocator data with satellite imagery to investigate how arrival and departure decisions throughout a bird’s migratory journey relate to seasonal changes in plant growth. Scientists have now tracked dozens of bird species with multisensor geolocators , and that number increases every year. Each mapped migratory journey improves our understanding of how small birds migrate, what factors shape their movements, and how best to protect them. items.titleOriginal: Kelly Clarkson sang a ghoulish version of the Bee Gees’ ‘Stayin’ Alive’ for Halloween
items.description: Το “Stayin’ Alive” των Bee Gees είναι ένα υπέροχο τραγούδι για πολλούς λόγους. items.descriptionOriginal: “Stayin’ Alive” by the Bee Gees is a great song for many reasons. It’s about survival in the big city, and its propulsive disco drumbeat is so close to a typical heartbeat that CPR instructors ask people to hum it in their heads while administering chest compressions . It seems that in 1977, with the song, the Bee Gees got to the core of what it means to be human and did so in amazing white silk pants. “[“Stayin’ Alive”] was based on Tony having a big night out in New York and the whole concept of being famous by dancing,” the Bee Gees’ Barry Gibb said, according to uDiscoverMusic . “The title came up real early on, but then the song started to evolve. The title is really what the song means about surviving on the streets, sort of a social comment.” Kelly Clarkson sings ‘Stayin’ Alive’ Talk show host Kelly Clarkson took the song’s meaning a step further by singing it in the Halloween edition of her Kellyoke segment. Clarkson sang it against a backdrop of bodies rising from the grave, turning the song’s meaning into an impassioned fight for her life. For this version, instead of surviving on the streets of New York City in the late ‘70s, Clarkson had to sing her way through a night of terror. For the performance, Clarkson dressed as Madeline Ashton, Meryl Streep’s character from 1992’s Death Becomes Her . At the beginning of the performance, she’s joined by background singers: one dressed as Goldie Hawn’s character and another as Ernest, who was played by Bruce Willis. “Look at this mansion, though! This is amazing, y’all. It’s just like the one Meryl lived in,” Clarkson said . “Those are actually the stairs Ernest pushed her down. There are the candelabras and, of course, Meryl’s portrait, which I’m seriously considering just keeping up year-round because I love her.” What’s interesting is that after a slowed-down intro, the song picks up the pace and gets an ‘80s Michael Jackson “Thriller” vibe, which lets Clarkson show off her powerful voice. Her take contrasts sharply with the falsetto sung by Barry Gibb and his brothers in the original version. Clarkson has never been quiet about her love for Meryl Streep To Clarkson fans, it’s not a huge surprise that she dressed up as a character from a Meryl Streep film; the talk show host hasn’t been quiet about her love for her. When Clarkson met Streep in 2018 at the Golden Globes, she told the Mamma Mia! star that she had been a huge fan of her since she was 8. In 2019, Clarkson launched an online campaign, #FromKellyToMeryl, to try to get Streep to appear on her show. Sadly, for Clarkson, it still hasn’t happened. Last year, Clarkson sang ‘I Put a Spell on You’ for Halloween In 2025, Clarkson dressed as Bette Midler from Hocus Pocus and gave a scorching performance of “I Put a Spell on You, originally popularized by Screamin’ Jay Hawkins. The post Kelly Clarkson sang a ghoulish version of the Bee Gees’ ‘Stayin’ Alive’ for Halloween appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Πώς οι πιστώσεις άνθρακα βοήθησαν να ξεκλειδωθεί το Εθνικό Πάρκο Great Koala στη NSW
items.titleOriginal: How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in NSW
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Το Εθνικό Πάρκο του Μεγάλου Κοάλα μπορεί να ακούγεται σαν ένα μέρος που είναι πολύ καλό για να είναι αληθινό, αλλά είναι αληθινό. Μετά από περισσότερο από μια δεκαετία προεκλογικής εκστρατείας, τρεις πολιτειακές εκλογές και πάνω από 14 ώρες κοινοβουλευτικής συζήτησης, η Νέα Νότια Ουαλία δημιούργησε το δεύτερο μεγαλύτερο εθνικό πάρκο της πολιτείας. Αποτελείται από 478.000 εκτάρια…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The Great Koala National Park might sound like a place that’s too good to be true, but it is real. After more than a decade of campaigning, three state elections, and over 14 hours of parliamentary debate, New South Wales has established the state’s second-largest national park. It’s made up of 478,000 hectares (about 1.2 million acres) between Kempsey and Grafton on the Mid North Coast. More than 100 species of flora and fauna will be protected within its boundaries. The park is a patchwork of existing protected areas stitched together with more than 178,000 hectares (roughly 440,000 acres) of former state forest and Crown Land. The legislation passed through approximately 160 amendments before it got there. The campaign started small. Conservationist Ashley Love began lobbying for the park after hearing from local residents that koalas in the region weren’t as common as they once were. “It became too much to ignore,” he said. What started as a proposal to protect Crown Land eventually became a Labor election platform. NSW Labor took it to the 2015 and 2019 elections, lost both, and won government in 2023 on a ticket that included the park. Carbon credits sealed the deal Carbon credits were central to making the legislation work. The federal Clean Energy Regulator registered a project covering more than 117,000 hectares (about 289,000 acres) of the park’s state forest areas. By formally ending native forest logging there, the government can now sell carbon credits from the land. Protected forest , it turns out, generates more revenue than logged timber. Of course, that trade-off still has real costs. The Forestry Corporation of NSW had already cut more than 30 jobs in Coffs Harbour as the logging moratorium ate into forward orders. Timber NSW president Andrew Hurford laid it out: “Staff have been laid off; engineering firms that provide support to those companies have no forward orders … downstream people supplying tyres, fuel, trucking, transport, engineering. All of those things are gradually becoming slower and quieter.” The government has committed to moving displaced Forestry Corporation staff into roles with the National Parks and Wildlife Service. A park with gaps still to close NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe called it “a defining moment for conservation in NSW,” and by the numbers, it qualifies. Love, whose decade of advocacy made the proposal viable, was more measured. “Its nature is quite fragmented, and there are gaps and connectivity issues between sections of it, but it is a big step forward,” he said. Koalas need connected habitat to move, breed, and survive disease pressure. A 478,000-hectare patchwork is still a meaningful step up from what existed. The carbon credit structure gives the protected land a financial rationale that most past conservation campaigns lacked entirely. Love says he’ll keep pushing for the sections that didn’t make it in. After a decade, that sounds less like frustration than a habit he’s not planning to break. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in NSW first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: J ust weeks after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated while speaking at a college last September, students gathered in a University of Michigan classroom to discuss freedom of speech. Sitting in a semicircle, they were listening to one another share their views when one of the attendees pulled a red MAGA hat from his bag and asked if it would be okay to wear it. The gesture could have turned into a confrontation. The discussion’s moderator, however, said he was free to put it on. “We were all just like, ‘Okay, that’s your belief [and] that’s totally fine,’” recalls Sarah-Catherine Jackson, the president of BridgeUSA at UMich, the organization hosting the meeting. Students participate in a workshop at the BridgeUSA annual summit. Courtesy of BridgeUSA BridgeUSA at UMich is the University of Michigan’s chapter of BridgeUSA, a student movement built around structured political dialogue, welcoming different views as long as they are expressed with basic respect. Instead of debating for a quick win, students explain their beliefs, listen to others and stay in the room without needing to reach agreement. The need for such spaces is clear, says BridgeUSA. A 2024 Knight Foundation-Ipsos study of more than 1,500 college students between the ages of 18 and 24 found that two in three said they self-censored on topics such as gender, religion, race and LGBTQ+ issues during classroom discussions. A similar proportion reported that they believed such self-censorship limited educationally valuable conversations on campus. With another tense election pulling the country in opposite directions, BridgeUSA is betting that depolarization starts with something simple: getting supposed rivals to sit down and actually hear each other out. BridgeUSA — which was founded in 2017 at UC Berkeley after protests over a conservative speaker turned violent — works to facilitate those conversations. The organization has grown rapidly, from that first chapter in 2017, to 24 by 2020 , to 146 today. At its national summit in Philadelphia this August, 250 students gathered for leadership and moderation training, and to connect with peers from different regions and political perspectives. In spring 2024, pro-Palestine protests erupted at Columbia University in New York, leading to intensified disputes over campus speech, safety and protest, and prompting some to ask whether students with opposing views should engage with one another at all. BridgeUSA CEO Manu Meel says that when the protests began, BridgeUSA only had a small presence at the university and no trained student leaders able to convene a dialogue. But a group of students believed that kind of conversation was sorely needed, so they established a BridgeUSA chapter and organized a discussion about Israel and Palestine, an event Meel says university administrators declined to support because they feared negative publicity. The students proceeded anyway, and within a year Bridge Columbia convened a gathering of at least 200 students. While considered successful, this experience highlighted BridgeUSA’s dependence on local leadership. BridgeUSA now emphasizes trying to support rapid-response dialogue immediately after campus violence, protests and other flashpoints where possible. Listening to political opponents takes courage on campuses where students feel pressure to demonstrate ideological loyalty, says Meel, adding: “I don’t think protest is any more courageous because everybody protests today.” Instead, he describes structured dialogue as “the new campus counterculture.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] While dialogue performs a distinct democratic function, says University of Virginia professor Rachel Wahl, who studies political dialogue, she is wary of setting conversation and protest against each other and asserts that public demonstration remains vital: “People who want to be in dialogue should consider protest an important form of political communication.” BridgeUSA plans to grow to 800 chapters (roughly a quarter of U.S. colleges) — a reach Meel says could help make dialogue a campus norm and give quieter students “social permission” to participate. To truly make an impact, Nicholas V. Longo, director of the Rutgers Democracy Lab, asserts that dialogue must also extend into the places and spaces where students already spend time. “Campuses need to not only engage students who are ready, but also students who might avoid these kinds of opportunities. We sometimes say we want to try to make engagement in dialogue unavoidable. To do this, we need to go to where students are at — in student centers, res life and first year experiences; but then also it’s essential to build these opportunities into the curriculum.” BridgeUSA CEO Manu Meel describes structured dialogue as the new campus counterculture. Courtesy of BridgeUSA Back at the University of Michigan, where chapter meetings typically draw 10 to 15 students, keeping conversations balanced takes deliberate effort. Jackson, a self-described fairly conservative student on a predominantly liberal campus, says executive board members with different political views review presentations and social posts for partisan framing, and flag language that appears to lean left or right. The midterms bring national stakes to Ann Arbor, the home of the university, where student turnout could help shape the outcome of the state’s competitive Senate race — and, with it, which party controls the chamber. But the measure of BridgeUSA’s success extends beyond election day, says Longo, who states that dialogue can build civic knowledge and lead to informed action. After the votes are counted, it can also help students “repair and rebuild” their communities, and work together, regardless of who wins. The post The Student Movement Addressing Campus Polarization Head On appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Όταν ο ήλιος βρίσκεται χαμηλά στον ορίζοντα, το φως του ταξιδεύει μέσα από ένα πολύ μεγαλύτερο τμήμα της ατμόσφαιρας πριν φτάσει στα μάτια μας. Μικροσκοπικό σωματίδιο…
items.descriptionOriginal: Cyclone Arnab turned Chhattisgarh’s sky blood red! But is it a warning sign or simply science? The answer lies in how sunlight travels through our atmosphere. Sunlight may look white, but it contains every colour. When the sun is low on the horizon, its light travels through a much longer stretch of atmosphere before reaching our eyes. Tiny particles in the air scatter shorter wavelengths, such as blue and violet, more strongly. Red and orange light travel through more easily, making sunsets appear dramatically colourful. During a cyclone, changing atmospheric conditions and increased moisture and airborne particles can influence how light scatters, creating striking red and orange skies. This phenomenon is connected to Rayleigh scattering, the science that helps explain why sunsets often appear red. So, a blood-red sky isn't automatically a bad omen or a danger warning. It's a fascinating reminder of how light and our atmosphere interact. items.description: Σε μέρη του Ταμίλ Ναντού, το Diwali έρχεται με έναν ασυνήθιστο κανόνα: αφήστε τα κροτίδες έξω. Ο λόγος κρέμεται ανάποδα στα δέντρα. Σε ορισμένα μέρη, το έθιμο είναι δεμένο με ιερό δέντρο ή τοπική θεότητα. Σε άλλα…
items.descriptionOriginal: In parts of Tamil Nadu, Diwali comes with an unusual rule: leave the firecrackers out . The reason hangs upside down in the trees. Hundreds of bats roost in village banyans and tamarinds. Rather than drive them away, residents have built traditions around protecting them. In some places, the custom is tied to a sacred tree or local deity. In others, it began with families feeding the animals. The stories are different, but the relationship is striking. These villagers do not see the bats as pests to chase away. They see them as neighbours, guests or even protectors, and have learnt to celebrate Diwali around their presence. The night shift that keeps nature growing When fruit bats leave their roosts after sunset, they begin a nightly journey in search of fruit and nectar. Their work, however, extends well beyond finding food. For generations, villagers have kept firecrackers away from their winged neighbours, protecting the bats that roost in their trees. All Photographs courtesy of: ( The Hindu ) As bats eat fruit, they disperse seeds across the landscape, helping plants regenerate in places where seeds might otherwise never reach. By feeding on nectar, some also pollinate flowers. These activities support the growth of trees and vegetation, which in turn provide food and shelter for other wildlife. Their daytime roosts are just as important. Large colonies often gather in the same trees, returning to familiar resting places after a night of foraging. Sudden, loud firecracker bursts and flashes of light can alarm bats and disturb their roosting behaviour. Repeated disturbance may cause them to abandon a tree and seek another place to rest. For the villages that share their landscape with these animals, keeping Diwali quiet is a simple way to reduce that disturbance. The family that climbed a tree to feed bats In Kazhuperumpakkam, near Vanur in Villupuram district, the story began with a tamarind tree. Families noticed bats gathering around it to feed on its fruit. Instead of driving them away, they began leaving food for the animals. The care went further. Men climbed the tree and placed a large vessel between its branches, filling it with water. Children watched the bats move around the tree and, as they grew older, continued the practice of feeding them. In Kazhuperumpakkam, a tradition of feeding bats grew into a community-wide effort to protect them. The village eventually took responsibility for protecting the animals. The panchayat banned firecrackers, and the practice continued even after the families who first cared for the bats moved away. The village has also faced a difficult side of conservation. Residents said the bat colony once numbered in the thousands, but hunting and disturbance led to a decline. The bats moved to another banyan tree after the old one lost branches. In Perambur, near Kollidam in Mayiladuthurai district, the relationship has a more spiritual connection. Hundreds of bats roost in a sprawling banyan tree called Vavvaal Thoppu , or the bat grove. A shrine dedicated to Lord Muneeswaran stands nearby, and residents consider the grove sacred. For more than a century, villagers have avoided firecrackers during Diwali. The festival is still celebrated, but residents gather at the Sri Aaladiamman temple instead of filling the night with fireworks. A father stopped his son from bursting crackers. Three generations followed. In Thoppupatti and Saampatti, in Tiruchirappalli district, hundreds of fruit bats roost in a large banyan tree near a statue of the village deity, Muniyappa Swamy. Residents believe the bats bring good fortune and protect the community. A father's decision to stop his son from bursting crackers in Kalapattu became a tradition carried forward through three generations. Dhanraj, a resident of Saampatti, told India Today that villagers avoid crackers because the noise disturbs the bats. He described watching them fly out in the evening and return by dawn as a sight that makes the village proud. In Kalapattu, near Katpadi, the custom has a personal memory attached to it. G Sampath recalled that when he was 12, his father stopped him from bursting crackers because bats roosted in the village's trees . The practice has continued for three generations. The village's protection goes beyond Diwali. Residents refuse to let outsiders catch or hunt the bats. Yet they make one exception: firecrackers are allowed during funeral ceremonies, when they are part of local rites. Sampath acknowledged that the noise may frighten the animals, but described it as unavoidable. Schoolchildren are learning to protect their winged neighbours At Kittampalayam, near Coimbatore, the effort to protect bats has reached the classroom. In November 2012, Government Middle School hosted a bat and bird conservation programme, introducing students to the animals that roost in their village. In Perambur, a sacred banyan tree shelters hundreds of bats, while residents celebrate Diwali without fireworks. The children learnt why bats matter and took part in an awareness rally alongside villagers, conservationists and personnel from a nearby Border Security Force base. The programme was part of a wider effort to protect a colony of around 2,000 Indian flying foxes that roosted in two banyan trees and a tamarind tree. Around 350 families had already agreed to avoid firecrackers during Diwali. The students helped carry that message beyond the school, encouraging the community to see the bats not as intruders, but as fellow inhabitants of the village. The programme gave children a way to connect what they learnt in class with the wildlife around their homes. By taking part in the rally, they helped carry the message beyond the school gates: protecting the bats meant protecting a part of their village that had shared its trees with them for generations. The bats are protected from crackers. But what about curious visitors? For these communities, protecting the bats also means guarding their roosts from hunting and disturbance. In Kazhuperumpakkam, villagers have spoken about outsiders catching bats. The community's decision to protect the roosts helps keep the animals from being treated as an easy target. At Kittampalayam, schoolchildren took the message of bat conservation beyond the classroom, encouraging hundreds of families to celebrate a quieter Diwali. In Kalapattu, residents have also refused to let outsiders catch or hunt the bats. Their protection is rooted in a custom passed down through generations, and in the belief that the animals belong in the village's trees. Perambur's Vavvaal Thoppu presents a different challenge. The banyan tree and its bats are closely tied to local belief, and some residents hope the grove can attract nature lovers. But visitors bring the possibility of noise and disruption. The question is how to welcome people without turning the bats' resting place into a spectacle. These villages have found a way to celebrate Diwali without asking their wild neighbours to leave. Sometimes, protecting wildlife begins with something as simple as choosing not to make a noise. Sources ' Choosing bats over fireworks: Coimbatore's Kittampalayam village leads the way this Deepavali too ': by Avantika Krishna for The Hindu, Published on 11 November, 2023 ' For over a century, these villagers have celebrated a noiseless Deepavali to protect bats ': by Express News Service for The New Indian Express, Published on 24 October, 2019 ' For this village in Tamil Nadu, it's bats over crackers on Deepavali ': by Antony Fernando for The New Indian Express, Published on 31 October, 2024 ' Tamil Nadu: These villages prefer silent Diwali to protect environment, bats and winged creatures ': by Lokpria Vasudevan for India Today, Published on 5 November, 2018

items.description: Μια σημαντική 24χρονη μελέτη που περιελάμβανε περισσότερους από 8.200 ενήλικες δείχνει ότι το υπερβολικό σωματικό βάρος μπορεί να επιταχύνει τη γήρανση του εγκεφάλου, οδηγώντας σε ταχύτερη μείωση της μνήμης, της συγκέντρωσης και των δεξιοτήτων λήψης αποφάσεων. Η σύνδεση ήταν ιδιαίτερα ισχυρή μεταξύ των ατόμων άνω των 65 ετών, προκαλώντας ανησυχίες για τις μακροπρόθεσμες επιπτώσεις της παχυσαρκίας στην υγεία του εγκεφάλου.
items.descriptionOriginal: A major 24-year study involving more than 8,200 adults suggests that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision-making skills. The connection was particularly strong among people over 65, raising concerns about the long-term effects of obesity on brain health.

items.descriptionOriginal: Mysterious particles called neutrinos constantly stream through our bodies, and scientists are now detecting incredibly powerful versions arriving from distant cosmic sources using a massive observatory buried in Antarctic ice. These elusive “ghost particles” could hold extraordinary clues about the Big Bang, extreme cosmic events, and some of the universe’s greatest mysteries.

At Stonecraft Woods Shamshabad, 18 acres of a 60-acre development have been dedicated to a Miyawaki forest. Home to 4.5 lakh native trees, 141 bird species and over 153 medicinal, aromatic, fruiting and flowering plant species, it offers a different perspective on how we build. From identifying native plant species to rescuing century-old trees, discover how this forest took shape. items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have developed a remarkable new electronic implant that could transform type 2 diabetes treatment by lowering blood sugar without insulin or traditional drugs. The device uses a special electrically powered catalyst to convert excess glucose into a substance that the body eliminates through urine, potentially preventing unwanted energy from being stored as fat. In diabetic mice, the implant precisely controlled blood sugar and promoted weight loss.

items.description: Για σχεδόν τρεις δεκαετίες, το καταφύγιο άγριας ζωής Kailadevi του Rajasthan δεν είχε τεκμηριωμένη επιτυχημένη αναπαραγωγή τίγρεων. items.descriptionOriginal: For nearly three decades, Rajasthan's Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary had no documented successful tiger breeding. Tigers passed through its forests, but could they raise cubs here again? That has finally changed. Over the past five years, eight cubs and three adult tigers have been recorded here, raising hopes of a breeding population beyond Ranthambore. The discovery is detailed in a new study by WWF-India and the Rajasthan Forest Department, released in Jaipur on 16 October 2026. What happens next matters. Why the birth of eight cubs matters Located in Rajasthan's Karauli district, Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary spreads across approximately 674 sq km of forests, rocky hills and deep ravines. Established in 1983, it forms the northern extension of Ranthambore Tiger Reserve. For tigers moving out of Ranthambore, these forests offer a route towards other wildlife habitats, including the Dholpur-Karauli Tiger Reserve and Madhya Pradesh's Kuno National Park. But a forest where a tiger can travel is different from one where it can raise cubs. A mother needs sheltered spaces to protect her young, enough wild animals to hunt and a suitable habitat where her cubs can grow. That is what makes the recent breeding records encouraging. They suggest that parts of Kailadevi are providing conditions in which tigers can reproduce. K C A Arun Prasad, Rajasthan's Chief Wildlife Warden, said, "Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary is emerging as a vital landscape for tiger conservation, with successful breeding after three decades." He believes protecting the forests and the routes connecting them could help establish a second breeding tiger population alongside Ranthambore. What 186 hidden cameras discovered To understand the wildlife living in Kailadevi, researchers from WWF-India and the Rajasthan Forest Department carried out a detailed assessment between November 2023 and February 2024. Striped hyenas were photographed most frequently among the larger meat-eating animals, followed by wolves and leopards Photograph: (WWF India) They collected usable records from 186 camera-trap stations placed across the sanctuary. These cameras automatically photographed animals passing through, helping researchers study wildlife that can be difficult to observe directly. The cameras recorded 27 mammal species, revealing the variety of animals sharing these forests. Among them were leopards. Researchers identified 29 individual leopards and estimated their density at approximately 3.65 per 100 sq km. Striped hyenas were photographed most frequently among the larger meat-eating animals, followed by wolves and leopards. Jackals, Indian foxes, jungle cats and caracals were also recorded. The team also studied plant-eating animals that serve as prey for tigers. Their numbers matter because breeding is only the beginning. As cubs grow, they need enough food and space to survive independently. Why these tigers need forests beyond Ranthambore As young tigers grow, they may leave their birth territories to find space of their own. For that journey, they need connected stretches of forest where they can move, find mates and establish new territories. This is where Kailadevi becomes particularly important. Its location helps connect Ranthambore with neighbouring wildlife habitats. But roads, expanding settlements and damage to forest patches can interrupt these routes, making movement difficult for animals. Conservationists will need to continue monitoring tigers, protecting forest connections and ensuring that enough wild prey remains available. Photograph: (Prashant Mahajan) Protecting these connections is therefore essential if Kailadevi is to support tigers over generations. And that work involves the people living around these forests. How nearby villages are helping protect the landscape WWF-India and Rajasthan Forest Department initiatives have benefited nearly 8,000 residents across 46 forest-fringe villages around Ranthambore and Kailadevi. These include livelihood support, cleaner energy options and programmes that involve people in protecting their surrounding forests. The aim is to meet local needs while reducing pressure on the habitat that wildlife depends on. Such work matters in places where people depend on the same forests that tigers and other wild animals need to survive. Can Kailadevi give these cubs a future? The return of tiger breeding is encouraging, but Kailadevi's recovery will depend on what happens next. Conservationists will need to continue monitoring tigers, protecting forest connections and ensuring that enough wild prey remains available. The eight cubs recorded over five years do not yet establish a secure, self-sustaining tiger population. They do, however, show why protecting this sanctuary matters. After nearly three decades without documented successful breeding , tigers are once again raising young in Kailadevi. With continued protection of its forests and support from the communities living around them, the sanctuary could become a home for future generations of tigers. Sources: 'New study finds Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary as a key stronghold for tiger recovery and wildlife conservation in Rajasthan' : WWF India Western India Conservation Landscape : WWF-India

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Sensory Food Education for Children in UK Schools Helps Pupils Enjoy Vegetables Reading Time: 3 minutes Sensory food education for children in UK schools and nurseries is fully funded, helping pupils learn to enjoy fruit and vegetables. The charity TastEd now fully funds sensory food education for children in UK schools and nurseries. It helps pupils learn to enjoy fruit and vegetables. Teachers need no kitchen or fancy equipment. The need is clear. In the UK, 79.1% of children aged 5 to 10 eat fewer than 3.5 portions of fruit and vegetables a day. In a class of 30 pupils, that is about 24 children. Put another way, only about 21% of children in that age group reach 3.5 portions. TastEd wants to change that through food lessons, using sensory food education for children in UK schools nationwide. The charity is registered in England and Wales and in Scotland. Pressure has not solved the problem. TastEd says cajoling, reward charts and 5-a-day messages have not raised intake. The 5-a-day message urges 5 portions of fruit and vegetables daily. Yet the average UK child eats just over 1 portion of vegetables a day. Why do children eat so few? TastEd points to a simple reason. Many children dislike vegetables and don’t know them well. The charity shares telling examples. It says some British 11-year-olds have never tried a raw tomato. Some 8-year-olds cannot recognize an onion. Sensory food education for children in UK schools, as delivered by teachers, is simple in practice. A teacher brings fresh fruit or vegetables into the classroom. Children talk and write about what they see, smell, touch, hear and taste. Children also say whether they enjoy the food. The setting is fun and pressure-free. TastEd says pupils often surprise themselves by enjoying foods they expected to dislike. TastEd calls taste education food education in its simplest form. It says the effect on children can be large. A course of lessons builds a taste for healthy foods and confidence in sharing preferences. Sensory food education for children in UK schools is simple in practice: a teacher brings in fresh fruit or vegetables, and children talk and write about what they see, smell, touch, hear, and taste in a fun, pressure-free setting. Photo by Yuliia Patrikhalkina on Pexels. The lessons follow the Sapere method. Many European countries have used it for decades. Evidence from Finland suggests children who receive taste education are more likely to try new vegetables, fruits and berries. The World Health Organization (WHO) backs a whole-school approach to healthy food. Its January 2026 guideline says healthy food in schools can help children build good eating habits for life. WHO estimates that 466 million children worldwide receive school meals. That fits the idea behind sensory food education for children in UK schools. Healthy habits begin early, and school is a practical place to start. Parents know the struggle. TastEd notes that giving children positive exposure to fruit and vegetables at home can be hard, especially with picky eaters. School lessons offer that exposure in a group setting. Schools also report that pupils become more adventurous with school lunches. That is a practical benefit for schools and families. Teachers get support, training and resources for sensory food education for children in UK schools. The lessons match the English National Curriculum and cover the food requirements of primary design and technology. They can also link to English, history and science. TastEd says the lessons need very few resources and no specialist knowledge. Any teacher can run them. The charity says its approach delivers the recommendations of the National Food Strategy, an independent review of England’s food system. Teachers share positive results. A reception teacher in Cambridge says the lessons build literacy skills and motivate pupils to write. A Lincolnshire teacher describes reluctant eaters becoming willing tasters over time. TastEd also explains why it is needed. It describes a worldwide child health crisis linked largely to diet. Fresh food can be costly, and some homes lack proper cooking facilities. The charity also notes that sugary foods are heavily marketed, while fresh home-made food is not. Classroom lessons give every participating child a chance to meet fresh produce. Parents and nurseries can join in too. Families can try at home with activities, lessons, and videos on the website. Activity clubs and childminders also have log-in options. Nurseries can use a dedicated page for the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS). EYFS is the framework for children from birth to age five in England. Primary schools have their own page. Other places are seeing similar results from fresh food in school. A statewide farm-to-school program in California now reaches 500 school districts and is a permanent policy. At one district, students line up for unfamiliar fruits such as rambutan. Primary schools and nurseries can sign up for sensory food education through the TastEd website. Access is fully funded. TastEd compares taste education to learning to read and write. It calls the skill food literacy, which helps children feel confident around food. What could sensory food education for children in UK schools change if every child learned it early? items.descriptionOriginal: A journalist spent the last year of his dying father's life doing what he had always done with strangers but never with the man who had hurt him most: asking real questions and listening without flinching. What he uncovered -- in recorded conversations, old photographs, and two weathered shoeboxes hidden in plain sight -- was a pattern of compounding grief, passed quietly from generation to generation: a boy who lost his father to a war, who then couldn't be a father, who raised a son he couldn't understand. "It's the kind of wound I now see can be passed, from generation to generation, from father to son," the writer reflects. The most devastating discovery came after his father died, when he opened the shoeboxes his father had begged him to burn -- love letters from a grandfather killed in Italy in 1944, full of tender plans for a boy he would never come home to raise. What the son found there wasn't an excuse for the distance between them, but something more rare: a reason, which turned out to be enough.

items.descriptionOriginal: In the cold, high-altitude region of Leh in Ladakh, land once considered barren is now producing one of the world's most expensive spices. Saffron flowers have begun blooming here in less than 30 days after planting, offering fresh hope for agriculture in a region where farming conditions can be challenging. The first blooms appeared on land recently restored under Project Him Sarovar , an experimental initiative launched by Ladakh Lieutenant Governor VK Saxena. The most interesting part of the experiment is that the saffron flowers appeared much earlier than expected. The crop typically takes nearly two months to bloom after plantation, but the flowers in Leh appeared in less than half that time. The experiment could open up new opportunities for high-value crop cultivation in Ladakh, potentially creating additional income sources for farmers, local entrepreneurs, and young people. From barren land to a saffron field The experiment began on 1 October 2026, when nearly 800 kg of premium Iranian saffron corms were planted across 4,000 square metres of land in Leh. In the cold, high-altitude region of Leh in Ladakh, land once considered barren is now producing one of the world's most expensive spices. Photograph: (Instagram @moneycontrolcom) These corms, which are underground structures similar to bulbs, help saffron plants grow and produce flowers. The plantation involved around 90,000 corms, making it a substantial trial for the region. The land was previously degraded and unsuitable for cultivation. It was restored under Project Him Sarovar. The saffron plantation was then taken up to see whether the crop could grow in Ladakh's high-altitude conditions. Within weeks, the barren stretch of land began showing signs of life. Although the crop generally takes close to two months to flower after plantation, the first blooms appeared in Leh in less than 30 days. The first harvest brings encouraging results When Saxena visited the experimental field on Sunday, 1 November, he got to see the first flowers for himself. The field was producing an average of 20 to 25 blooming flowers each day. On the morning of his visit, the number reached 72, marking the highest daily count recorded so far. The team had also managed to collect nearly 22 grams of pure saffron over four days. While this is still a small harvest, it is an encouraging start for a crop being tested in a region where it has not traditionally been cultivated at this scale. The administration is now looking at how the plants perform under local conditions and whether the results can be sustained beyond this initial flowering period. Why saffron could be a valuable crop This crop is among the world's most expensive spices. It is widely used in cooking and traditional preparations, and its high market value makes it an attractive crop for farmers who can grow it successfully. India's saffron production is largely concentrated in Jammu and Kashmir, which accounts for approximately 90 percent of the country's total output. For farmers in Ladakh, cultivating saffron could offer another way to earn from their land. Instead of depending only on traditional agricultural practices, they could potentially grow a high-value crop with the opportunity to fetch better returns. The administration hopes the experiment will help diversify farming in the region, improve farmers' incomes and create opportunities for young people interested in agriculture and entrepreneurship. The experiment began on 1 October 2026, when nearly 800 kg of premium Iranian saffron corms were planted across 4,000 square metres of land in Leh. Photograph: (Instagram @moneycontrolcom) However, the project is still at the pilot stage. The first blooms are a positive sign , but further trials will be needed to establish whether the crop can be grown consistently and profitably on a commercial scale. Building on Ladakh's floriculture success This is not the first time the administration has experimented with high-value flower cultivation in Ladakh. Earlier, it undertook large-scale experiments with lilium and gladiolus in Leh. These flowers helped create livelihood opportunities for farmers, self-help groups, and local entrepreneurs. The success of these initiatives encouraged the administration to look at other crops that could grow in the region and offer better economic returns. Saffron is the latest addition to these efforts. If the ongoing trial proves successful, its cultivation could give local farmers another option beyond conventional crops and encourage the growth of small agro-based businesses. The Agriculture Department of the Union Territory of Ladakh and the field staff involved in the project have been acknowledged by the Lieutenant Governor for their work in bringing the experiment to life. For now, the 4,000-square-metre field in Leh offers an encouraging glimpse of what may be possible . Nearly 90,000 corms planted on restored land have already produced their first flowers, with the first saffron harvest following soon after. The field was producing an average of 20 to 25 blooming flowers each day. Photograph: (NDTV) Whether this experiment can eventually grow into a commercial farming opportunity remains to be seen. But for a region constantly finding ways to make agriculture more viable, these early blooms have given farmers and the administration something new to look forward to.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Global Soil Restoration Movement Reaches 4 Billion People Across 193 Nations Reading Time: 3 minutes A global soil restoration movement, launched through a 30,000-kilometer motorcycle journey, has reached an estimated 4 billion people and is pushing nations toward policies that protect agricultural soil from irreversible degradation. Save Soil , the movement behind this global push, centers on a stark warning: soil with insufficient organic content essentially turns to sand, triggering cascading consequences for food security, water systems, biodiversity, and climate stability. Currently, 52% of agricultural soils worldwide are classified as degraded, a figure that underscores the urgency behind what has become one of the largest environmental awareness campaigns in recent history. The soil restoration movement was founded by Indian yogi and environmental activist Sadhguru, who embarked on a 100-day motorcycle journey spanning 27 countries and 30,000 kilometers from the United Kingdom to India to raise awareness. That journey became the foundation for a campaign claiming to have reached 4 billion people, roughly 60% of the world’s electorate, through 691 events and interviews, more than 8,970 media stories, and 50 iconic landmarks illuminated worldwide in support of the cause. At the core of the soil restoration movement is a specific, measurable goal: restoring at least 3% to 6% organic matter in agricultural soil by shading land and enriching it with plant litter and animal waste. The movement outlines a three-pronged policy strategy presented at the UN Convention to Combat Desertification’s COP15: incentivizing farmers to increase soil organic matter, making carbon credits more accessible to farming communities, and establishing preferential marketing for produce grown in healthier, higher-organic-matter soil. The soil restoration movement aims to restore 3% to 6% organic matter in agricultural soil, which can hold up to 90% of its weight in water, addressing a crisis in which 52% of agricultural soils worldwide are already degraded. Photo by Tom Fisk on Pexels. The stakes extend across multiple interconnected crises. Degraded soils cannot adequately absorb and regulate water flows, contributing to droughts and floods alike, while organic-rich soil can hold up to 90% of its weight in water and release it gradually over time. Soil also stores roughly three times more carbon than living plants and twice as much as the atmosphere, meaning continued degradation risks releasing roughly 850 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, more than three decades of combined global emissions. The soil restoration movement has secured formal commitments from national governments through Soil Health memoranda of understanding, with countries including Azerbaijan, Romania, Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Suriname, Dominica, St. Lucia, St. Kitts and Nevis, Guyana, and the United Arab Emirates signing agreements committing to policies restoring and safeguarding soil health. The Caribbean region, in particular, has shown unified support, with multiple island nations joining within the same campaign cycle. Across North America, the soil restoration movement gained traction at the municipal level, with more than 150 cities proclaiming March 21 as Save Soil Day, including Washington, D.C., Austin, San Diego, Baltimore, Philadelphia, Phoenix, and dozens of smaller municipalities across the United States and Canada. These proclamations, while largely symbolic, reflect growing local government engagement with soil health as a civic priority rather than a purely agricultural concern. International institutions have also voiced support. The United Nations Environment Programme, the Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Health Organization, the World Food Programme, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature have all publicly backed the soil restoration movement’s objectives, alongside the Inter-American Institute for Cooperation on Agriculture and the Commonwealth of Nations. The campaign explicitly compares itself to a previous global environmental success story: the 1987 Montreal Protocol, through which 197 countries agreed to phase out ozone-depleting chemicals after confirming the Antarctic ozone hole. That agreement eliminated 99% of ozone-depleting substances, and current projections suggest the ozone layer will fully recover by mid-century. The soil restoration movement positions this precedent as proof that coordinated international policy can reverse seemingly intractable environmental crises when sufficient public and governmental will exists. Beyond policy advocacy, the soil restoration movement has catalogued more than 1,000 sustainable soil management solutions spanning 193 nations, alongside engaging younger generations directly, with 3 million children reportedly writing letters to their national leaders advocating for soil health policies. Recent reporting connected to the movement has also highlighted soil degradation’s role as a driver of global migration, with projections suggesting human displacement could double by the century’s end as soil degradation, climate change, and food insecurity compound one another. Land-related conflicts have already played a significant role in most major wars across Africa since 1990, underscoring how soil health intersects with geopolitical stability far beyond agricultural productivity alone. As the soil restoration movement continues expanding its policy reach, its core argument remains consistent: thriving soil policies require public support, and public support requires sustained awareness. Whether this translates into a binding international framework like the one that reversed ozone depletion remains to be seen, but the scale of global engagement so far suggests soil health has moved from a niche agricultural concern to a mainstream environmental and public health priority. The post Global Soil Restoration Movement Reaches 4 Billion People Across 193 Nations appeared first on Happy Eco News .
